issues.summary: The plan does not address how it will detect or control for temporal drift in transcript collection, speaker turnover (CFO changes), or IR coaching that may change tone independent of business fundamentals.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan requires 'within-firm, within-speaker baselines' to control for individual style, but it does not say how to handle speaker turnover. If a CFO retires and is replaced by someone younger, who talks more cautiously, the new person's deflection score on vendor topics is elevated compared to the firm baseline. Is that a signal that the deal is harder, or that the speaker is more cautious? The plan falls back to 'firm-level baseline on turnover, flagged low-confidence,' which is good, but 'flagged low-confidence' is not a control — it is a note saying 'this observation may be bad.' A study that includes flagged-low-confidence observations with a note that they are bad is a study that includes bad data. The plan also mentions 'signal decay post-2018 as IR adapts' in pitfalls — meaning vendors and firms know analysts are listening for tone and may be coached to sound evasive regardless of deal terms — but does not describe a mitigation.
issues.what_breaks: H1 and H2. If speaker turnover creates time-varying baseline shifts that are unmodeled, or if IR coaching (post-2018) has decoupled evasiveness from deal hardness, then the signal is period-dependent: valid pre-2018, worthless post-2018. The historical test will show a decaying coefficient in post-2018 subsample if this is true, but the plan does not state what counts as 'too much decay.' Is a coefficient that shrinks by 50% in the out-of-sample period (2017–present) a failure? The plan does not pre-commit.
issues.fix: Pre-specify: (1) How speaker turnover is handled — exclude low-baseline-coverage observations or apply a time-varying control for 'speaker tenure at firm' or 'speaker appearance count in trailing N quarters'? (2) Test for decay explicitly: Fit on 2005–2016, test 2017–2019 (early post period) and 2020–present (late post period). Report coefficients separately. Pre-commit: if the coefficient shrinks by >40% in the late period vs. early, the signal is fading and H2 is not met, even if the pooled t-stat is ≥2.5.

issues.summary: The plan uses a pre-fitted, pinned LLM at temp 0 for deflection scoring, but does not specify the model, whether it was fine-tuned on financial data, or how to reproduce it if the vendor updates it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan says: 'one pinned embedding model, one pinned LLM at temp 0.' But LLMs change (GPT-4 to GPT-5), and a study run on a specific model version is not reproducible once that version is retired. Additionally, a generic LLM (not fine-tuned on financial-earnings-call data) may not score 'deflection' the same way a human rater or a financial-domain model would. The plan tests inter-rater agreement on 1,000 hand-labels, but if the 1,000 labels were used to fine-tune the LLM, this is not a test of the LLM's accuracy; it is a test that the LLM memorized its training data.
issues.what_breaks: Reproducibility and robustness. A future analyst trying to replicate the study will not be able to use the same LLM, so the results cannot be reproduced. Additionally, if the LLM's training data includes financial earnings calls, there is a risk of data leakage: the LLM may have seen the same calls in pretraining and is scoring them based on memorized patterns, not on learned reasoning.
issues.fix: Specify: (a) Exact model name and version (e.g., 'gpt-3.5-turbo, version 0613'); (b) Whether the model was fine-tuned and on what data; (c) A mechanism for preserving the model and results if the vendor updates it (e.g., open-source a fine-tuned version, or use a version-controlled cloud service that archives the model state). (d) If the hand-labels are used for fine-tuning, split: 800 labels for fine-tune, 200 for test, and report accuracy on the 200. Do not report accuracy on data the model has seen.

issues.summary: The plan includes a source-robustness check (200-call overlap between Refinitiv and a second vendor) but does not specify what the second vendor is or how different it may be.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan mentions 'a 200-call overlap sample from a second vendor for a source-robustness check' and later 'transcript-source correlation must exceed 0.9 or drop affected components.' But it does not say which vendor. If it is another vendor of cleaned transcripts (e.g., Seeking Alpha), the check is meaningful. If it is human-transcribed notes (e.g., sell-side equity research), the two are not the same and a 0.9 correlation is a very high bar. The robustness check is only as strong as the second source is independent.
issues.what_breaks: Validation step. If the second vendor is not specified or is not independent, the robustness check does not confirm anything; it just shows that Refinitiv is consistent with Refinitiv-adjacent sources.
issues.fix: Name the second vendor upfront. If it is Seeking Alpha, CIQ, or another major vendor, specify what format (full transcript, analyst notes, Q&A only) and how the overlap sample of 200 calls is selected (random sample, or stratified by sector/period). Report the 0.9 threshold result explicitly: If transcript-source correlation is 0.92, report 'passed'; if 0.87, report 'narrow miss, investigate component with lowest correlation' or 'failed, discuss why.'

issues.summary: The plan's H2 claims a causal link from evasiveness to margin surprise, but is structured as a Granger-causality (lagged predictor of outcome), which only establishes sequencing, not causation.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan regresses 'GM surprise at t+1 to t+4' on 'ΔScore at t' and interprets this as evidence that evasiveness *reveals* vendor risk. But a lagged regression is not a causal identification. It is consistent with evasiveness being caused by an earlier shock (e.g., the announcement of a customer concentration increase) that then shows up as a margin surprise. The plan includes a 'reverse-causality control: condition on GM surprise/stock reaction at t,' which is good — it says 'if the margin surprise happened before the call, the call's evasiveness is not predictive' — but conditioning on a prior period's surprise does not establish that evasiveness is *causal* to the later surprise, only that it is not immediately responsive to the same shock.
issues.what_breaks: H2 interpretation. The plan reports 'ΔScore predicts margin surprise' as if the evasiveness is informative about margins. But if both evasiveness and margin surprise are caused by a third variable (e.g., customer churn, visible to management but not yet to analysts), the regression shows correlation, not causation, and the signal may not survive competitive discovery.
issues.fix: Add a placebo test that the plan nominally includes but does not elaborate: Does ΔScore on *non-vendor* topics (FX, headcount, buybacks) predict vendor-deal margins? If not, the specificity of the signal is confirmed (it is vendor-specific, not general pessimism). Additionally, in the write-up, frame the result as 'evasiveness is associated with and predictive of margin surprise, consistent with management knowledge of deal hardness revealing before margins move' rather than 'evasiveness causes margin surprise.'

issues.summary: The plan does not specify what happens if the 40,000-firm-quarter panel is unbalanced or has missing data on key variables, or how many firm-quarters are dropped due to missing Visible Alpha consensus or incident tags.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan says 'regress GM surprise on ΔScore' but does not define the final analysis sample. If 20% of firm-quarters are dropped because Visible Alpha has no consensus, or because the call had <3 vendor-topic exchanges, the stated sample size is misleading. The effective N is what matters for the t-statistic, not the number of unique firm-quarters in the raw panel.
issues.what_breaks: H2 test. A low effective N can inflate p-values (if the test is underpowered, hitting |t|≥2.5 is harder, but if achieved it is less trustworthy). Alternatively, if droppage is selective (e.g., smaller firms or recent periods are dropped more often), the final sample is not a representative test of the hypothesis.
issues.fix: Pre-specify the sample selection: Start with [X] firm-quarters, drop for [missing Visible Alpha consensus, missing call transcript, <3 vendor exchanges], resulting in [Y] firm-quarters. Report Y/X as a percentage. Re-run the analysis sample this to ensure it is representative (compare mean market cap, sector distribution, period coverage before and after). Report effective N in the regression output.

issues.summary: The plan aims to detect 15bp negative margin surprise at |t|≥2.5 in a cross-section, but does not discuss whether 15bp surprises are even observable after consensus is updated intra-quarter or post-quarter.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A 15bp margin surprise is small — about 0.1–0.2% of revenue for typical company margins. Consensus revisions happen continuously; by the time the quarterly earnings are released, most surprises are already priced into consensus. If the plan is trying to predict margin surprises that are *not already in consensus*, the surprise-surprise is the shock *after* the most recent consensus update. But consensus is updated whenever an analyst changes their estimate, which can happen weeks or months before the earnings release. A call happens after the previous quarter closes but before consensus updates for the current quarter. So evasiveness on Q2 call (end of Q2) predicts margin surprise in Q3 (released 4-6 weeks after Q2 call), but consensus for Q3 is already forming and Q2 revisions are already priced. The plan does not unpack this timing.
issues.what_breaks: H2 test and economic value. If the 15bp surprise is the realization minus the most-recent consensus, and if consensus is updated before the call becomes public (institutional clients get transcripts first), the signal may not be tradeable. Alternatively, if the surprise is measured against the first-day consensus for that quarter (a specific point-in-time), the plan has a cleaner measure but needs to specify.
issues.fix: Pre-specify: margin surprise = [actual GM reported in earnings] minus [Visible Alpha consensus as of X date], where X is defined as (a) the day before the earnings release, or (b) a fixed date 3 weeks before (simulating a trader who acts on the call without future consensus updates). Report the surprises statistics (mean, SD, decile breakdowns) to show the distributions are large enough to be economically meaningful. If the median surprise is <5bp, the signal is too small to trade.

issues.summary: The plan includes whole-call negative-word share as a control but does not distinguish between negative words on vendor topics (collinear with ΔScore) and negative words on other topics (a genuine control for general pessimism).
issues.why_it_applies_here: A control for 'whole-call negative-word share' could be measuring the same evasiveness on vendor topics if the negativity is concentrated there. If 50% of the call's negative words are on vendor topics, the whole-call negative-word control is collinear with the main regressor, and the coefficient on ΔScore is biased.
issues.what_breaks: H2 regression. If ΔScore and whole-call negative-word share are correlated >0.7, including both is mechanically unstable (high VIF) and the coefficient on ΔScore is not trustworthy.
issues.fix: Compute correlation between ΔScore and whole-call negative-word share. If >0.6, do not use whole-call as a control. Instead: control for negative-word share on *non-vendor* topics (proxy for general pessimism), leaving the vendor-specific negativity in the ΔScore.

issues.summary: The plan will report margin-surprise prediction (H2) and return prediction separately, but does not establish which one the original business question is asking for.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan says 'report margin-prediction and return-prediction outcomes side by side, since a signal with no return predictability is correct but worthless.' This is important insight, but the original question is 'Is the vendor risk *underpriced*,' which is a return question. Margins can surprise negatively and the stock can still not move (already priced, or offset by a buyback or better-than-expected tax rate). The plan will deliver both, which is good, but it does not pre-commit to a decision rule: Does H2 require margin-surprise prediction, or return prediction, or both? If only margins, the study succeeds even if the signal has no trading value.
issues.what_breaks: The verdict. The IC will see 'margins predicted, returns not predicted' and ask 'so what?' The answer is either (a) 'we learned how the business works even if the market prices it,' which is a capability-build finding, not an investment finding, or (b) 'we need to dig deeper into why margins do not predict returns,' which is a different study. Without a pre-committed rule, the landing is ambiguous.
issues.fix: Pre-specify: H2 success requires [margin-surprise prediction with |t|≥2.5 OR return prediction with |t|≥2.0, whichever is stricter] or [both]. Clearly state which. If the goal is to inform the one-name decision on vendor risk, return prediction is more relevant; if the goal is to build a margin-forecasting signal, margin prediction is the target.

issues.summary: The plan proposes Driscoll–Kraay standard errors for two-way clustering plus block bootstrap, but does not justify why both are needed or how they interact.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan says 'regress GM surprise on ΔScore with firm and quarter FE, controls, two-way clustered SEs plus Driscoll–Kraay. Block-bootstrap (2,000 draws) per call.' Driscoll–Kraay is typically used for panel data with both cross-sectional and time-series dependence, addressing spatial and temporal correlation. Two-way clustering (on firm and quarter) also addresses this. Block-bootstrap is a resampling method for inference. Using all three together is over-engineering: Driscoll–Kraay + two-way clustering are often substitutes, not complements. Block-bootstrap can validate SEs if the data is heavily non-normal, but quarterly earnings margins are not extreme, so the gain may be small.
issues.what_breaks: Inference and explainability. If Driscoll–Kraay, two-way clustering, and bootstrap all give similar SEs, the report is redundant. If they diverge, which one does the analyst report? If the analyst reports all three and they rank differently (e.g., Driscoll–Kraay: |t|=2.6, two-way: |t|=2.3, bootstrap: |t|=2.1), the IC will distrust all of them.
issues.fix: Pre-commit to one SE method. If the panel is balanced and time-series correlation is the main concern (quarters are adjacent), use Driscoll–Kraay. If the panel is unbalanced or there is significant within-firm clustering, use two-way clustering. Report SEs with and without firm/quarter FE to show the fixed effects are not mechanically driving the result, but do not report three different SE corrections. Bootstrap can be a robustness check (reported in an appendix) if the primary SEs are tight.

issues.summary: The plan defines success for H1 as evasiveness ≥1.5 SD above baseline, but does not justify why 1.5 SD, or whether this threshold varies by company size, sector, or call complexity.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A 1.5 SD threshold is a reasonable default (roughly p<0.07 in a normal distribution), but the plan does not explain the choice. Is it 1.5 because that is the convention in NLP evasiveness work? Because a pilot test showed it discriminates well? Or because it is a round number? For a concentrated long-only manager, a 1.5 SD elevation is a strong signal, but the plan does not acknowledge the Type I risk: false positives at this threshold may still lead to a bad call on this specific company. The plan does not adjust the threshold based on company size or sector (e.g., tech companies might sound more cautious due to IP concerns, commodities companies more cautious due to pricing volatility).
issues.what_breaks: H1 measurement. If the threshold is arbitrary, the definition of 'evasive call' is arbitrary, and H1 is not a stable hypothesis. Additionally, if the threshold is too tight, almost no calls meet it (false negatives); if too loose, many false positives.
issues.fix: Pre-specify the threshold using a pilot: Hand-audit 50–100 calls on vendor topics and score evasiveness 0–5. Compute the correlation with the SD-above-baseline score. Choose a threshold such that 'calls ≥threshold' have median hand-evasiveness ≥3.5 and calls <threshold have median <3. This ties the statistical definition to a human judgment and makes it defensible.

issues.summary: The plan is written as a single-analyst project over 4+ months, but does not name an owner, a reviewer (separate from the analyst), or a timeline with milestones.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A research plan without named ownership is a plan that can be abandoned or deprioritized. An analyst writing this plan owns the analysis, but who is checking the work? The IC is the final audience, not the checkpoint. For a five-person shop, the two PMs should be acting as reviewers, and the plan should specify that the PM reviews output at (e.g.) step 3 (validation of the classifier on hand-labels) before the analyst spends a month on the historical regression.
issues.what_breaks: Execution and course correction. If the analyst completes the classifier validation and the PM sees that precision is 0.82 (below the pre-set 0.85 target), the PM can ask the analyst to refine the tag-set. But if this review is not built into the timeline, the analyst may have already fit the regression and will be reluctant to go back.
issues.fix: Name: Analyst = [X], PM reviewer = [Y], timeline with checkpoints: [Week 2: data ingestion complete, [Y] reviews sample of 20 parsed calls], [Week 5: hand-labels completed, [Y] spot-checks 10 labels and reviews inter-rater agreement], [Week 8: classifier validation, [Y] reviews precision/recall on test set], [Week 12: regression output, [Y] reviews coefficient, t-stat, residuals before presentation to IC].

issues.summary: The plan does not address what to do if evasiveness is elevated in the call immediately before the renegotiation is announced (i.e., the market is not surprised), which would make the signal uninformative.
issues.why_it_applies_here: If a company announces a vendor renegotiation in a call, and the previous call (before the announcement) shows elevated evasiveness, the market should have already priced the renegotiation-related risk. The ΔScore from the pre-announcement call would predict the margin surprise, but the margin surprise would already be baked into the stock price. The plan's H2 tests whether evasiveness predicts margin surprise, but does not control for whether evasiveness predicted the stock's reaction before the call (i.e., whether the market had already inferred the issue). A robust falsifier would be: 'If evasiveness predicts margins and the market has not already priced it, the stock should drift following calls with elevated evasiveness.' The plan includes CRSP CAR around next print, which is related, but does not specify what counts as 'the market already priced it.'
issues.what_breaks: Economic value and generalization of H2. If evasiveness is only predictive of margin surprises that are already known to the market (either because they were inferred from prior calls or disclosed explicitly), the signal is not investable, even if statistically significant.
issues.fix: Add a test: For firms with elevated ΔScore in call t, measure cumulative abnormal return (CAR) from call-date to earnings-date (t+1 Q) and compare to firms with low ΔScore. If CAR is similar (both drift positive or drift negative), the market is responding equally and the signal has no alpha. If high-ΔScore firms drift more negative, the signal reveals un-priced information. Pre-commit which result would count as falsification: if CAR is not significantly different, the signal is priced and H2 is a side effect, not the mechanism.

issues.summary: The plan specifies that vendor exchanges require '≥150 words or report insufficient evidence,' but does not justify the 150-word threshold or show that evasiveness is measurable at smaller sizes.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A management answer of 145 words is dropped as 'insufficient evidence.' But evasiveness can be communicated in fewer words: 'I cannot comment on that' (3 words) is highly evasive. Requiring ≥150 words biases the sample toward verbose calls and may miss the most evasive responses (which are often brief). The threshold is likely set to ensure the linguistic features (Loughran–McDonald word counts, etc.) have enough data to compute, but if so, it should be stated.
issues.what_breaks: H1 measurement. If the 150-word threshold drops the most-evasive responses, the sample is truncated on the dependent variable, and the ΔScore is underestimating true evasiveness variation. This is a form of selection bias.
issues.fix: Pre-test the linguistic features on short responses: Compute hedging, deflection, specificity, etc. on responses of 50 words, 100 words, 150 words. Show that the features are stable (correlation >0.8) across these ranges. If they are, lower the threshold or drop it. If they are unstable, keep the threshold but note that it introduces selection bias and report results stratified by answer length (separate analysis for ≥150 word vs. 150 words, if sample is large enough).

issues.summary: The plan assumes management's evasiveness is informative about vendor-deal hardness, but does not account for the possibility that the CFO is simply bad at public speaking or that the call environment (analyst aggression, time pressure) causes all executives to sound evasive.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan controls for 'within-speaker baselines' (each executive's typical deflection rate) and 'within-call baselines' (the same executive on other topics in the same call), which is smart. But if the entire call is unusually evasive — many topic-switches, defensive tone, shorter answers — the within-call baseline shifts, and the vendor-topic ΔScore becomes a residual that is hard to interpret. The plan does not explicitly address call-environment confounds: Was the call unusual in any way (new CFO, scandal, short quarter, etc.)? Did analysts ask unusually tough questions on vendor topics (which would provoke defensiveness regardless of deal hardness)?
issues.what_breaks: H1 measurement. If the within-call, within-speaker baseline is already elevated due to call environment, the ΔScore is understated. Conversely, if the overall baseline is depressed (calm call), the ΔScore is overstated. The plan flags these cases as 'low-confidence' but includes them in the analysis.
issues.fix: Add a control: 'call volatility' = SD of evasiveness across all topics in that call. If a call's overall evasiveness is very high, flag it. Then run H2 with and without high-volatility calls. If the coefficient on ΔScore shrinks materially when high-volatility calls are excluded, the effect is partially driven by call environment, not vendor-specific evasiveness. Report this explicitly.

issues.summary: The plan sets a ≥5pp improvement over base rate for sign-prediction (calling margin surprise direction) but computes this on the same sample where the model was fit (not out-of-sample), if 'blind human rating' means validation on a separate hold-out set (which is unclear).
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan says 'strict out-of-sample split (fit 2005–2016, test 2017–present, no refitting, no look-ahead),' which is good. But then it also mentions 'blind human rating (200 exchanges, ρ≥0.6)' which is for validating the exchange-tagging, not the H2 test. The H2 test (does ΔScore predict margin surprise?) is done on the 2017–present test set, and the plan pre-commits to |t|≥2.5 and ≥5pp improvement over base rate. But what is the base rate: (a) the base rate in the test set? (b) a benchmark model fit on the training set and applied to test? (c) a random guess (50%)? The plan does not specify, which matters for the 5pp threshold.
issues.what_breaks: H2 success criterion. If base rate is computed on the test set (e.g., 52% of test-set firm-quarters have negative margin surprises), then a model that always predicts negative gets 52% accuracy and passes the test. If base rate is a benchmark model (e.g., a logit fit on 2005–2016 and applied to 2017–present), the 5pp improvement must beat that benchmark. These are very different thresholds.
issues.fix: Pre-specify: base rate = [empirical frequency of ≥15bp negative GM surprise in test set, 2017–present] = [X%]. Success criterion: sign-prediction accuracy on test set ≥ X% + 5pp. Alternatively, use a benchmark model (e.g., logit on lagged margin level + revenue surprise + sector trend) fit on training, applied to test, and require H2 model to have 5pp better accuracy than benchmark.

issues.summary: The plan's core hypothesis requires that management knows the vendor deal will be hard (which is why they sound evasive), but if the deal outcome is not yet determined at call time, the evasiveness is speculative and uninformative.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A vendor renegotiation is a negotiation. At the time of the earnings call, the terms may not be finalized. Management may sound evasive because (a) they know the deal is hard and it will hurt margins, or (b) they are in the middle of negotiations and cannot disclose yet, or (c) they are optimistic but cannot promise anything until it is signed. The hypothesis that evasiveness = knowledge of hardness assumes (a), but (b) and (c) are equally consistent with evasiveness. Post-call, the deal closes. Did it hurt margins? If it did not, the evasiveness was about negotiating uncertainty, not hidden downside.
issues.what_breaks: Causal inference in H2. Even if evasiveness predicts margin surprise in a regression, the causal channel is ambiguous. The plan includes a check (reverse-causality control: condition on prior-period margin surprise or stock reaction) but does not address whether evasiveness reflects actual knowledge or just uncertainty. A robust check would be: post-deal-close calls, where the renegotiation is resolved, management should be more specific (less evasive) *and* should describe the outcome (better or worse margins). If post-deal-close calls still show elevated evasiveness on the topic (or if evasiveness on post-resolution calls does not correlate with actual deal outcome), the evasiveness is not informative.
issues.fix: Add a known-outcome validation (planned as step 6, should be step 1): Collect 20–30 renegotiation calls where the renegotiation is resolved and margin impact is known. Compute ΔScore on the pre-resolution call. Check if ΔScore correlates with actual margin impact (Spearman ρ >0.4 at minimum). If correlation is weak, evasiveness does not track deal hardness; stop. If strong, the hypothesis is validated on a small sample and proceeding to the broad panel is justified.

issues.summary: The plan proposes analyzing earnings calls dating back to 2005, but does not acknowledge that transcript quality, speaker identification, and analyst coverage have changed dramatically over that period, especially pre-2010 and post-2015 (due to IR professionalization).
issues.why_it_applies_here: Transcripts from 2005–2010 are often hand-transcribed with errors, speaker IDs are inconsistent, and companies did not have professional IR teams coaching tone. Post-2015, especially after Reg FD clarifications and social media scrutiny, IR teams are coached on tone and messaging consistency. This means the relationship between evasiveness and fundamental risk may be unstable across the period: pre-2010, evasiveness is less shaped by coaching and more tied to business conditions; post-2015, evasiveness is more a function of IR practice and less informative. The plan mentions 'signal decay post-2018 as IR adapts' but does not address the longer trend.
issues.what_breaks: H2 regression. If the relationship between evasiveness and margin surprise is period-dependent (stronger pre-2010, weaker post-2015), the pooled coefficient is unstable. The test set (2017–present) is entirely in the post-IR-professionalization period, so the effect may not replicate in the training set.
issues.fix: Run H2 stratified by 2005–2010, 2011–2015, 2016–present, and report coefficients for each period. If the effect is concentrated in the early period, the signal may not work going forward and H2 should be reframed as 'worked historically but unlikely to work now.' If the effect is stable, report that explicitly and use it to defend the hypothesis going forward.

issues.summary: The plan does not quantify the cost (analyst time, data licensing, compute) or the required precision (how good does the evasiveness measure need to be) for the one-name decision to change.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A five-person manager with one analyst should not commit 3–4 months of effort (and compute + licensing costs) unless the work changes the decision on the company. The plan does not state: 'If evasiveness is ≥1.5 SD above baseline, I will increase the position size / reduce the position / initiate a new position,' nor does it state what the cost of being wrong is. A 15bp margin surprise is a material but not transformative finding ($400m AUM, 2–3% position = $8–12M, 15bp margin surprise = $1.2–1.8M gross impact). If the analyst's time costs the firm $500k (3–4 months × $150k/yr salary + benefits), the ROI depends on how confident the decision is and how much capital can be moved as a result.
issues.what_breaks: The business case. A capability-build project (learning whether evasiveness predicts margins broadly) is not the same as a one-name decision project (should we bet on this company's vendor risk?). If the plan is framed as the former, it is an allocation decision (invest in research infrastructure), not an investment decision. If it is framed as the latter, the plan is over-engineered and mis-scoped.
issues.fix: Explicitly state: 'This work is [capability-build / one-name decision] and if [success criterion], we will [action].' If capability-build, the success criterion is 'can we measure evasiveness and does it predict margins broadly,' the timeline is 6–9 months, and the outcome is 'a tool we can apply to future positions.' If one-name decision, the success criterion is 'does this company sound more evasive than baseline, and does that imply margin risk,' the timeline is 2–3 weeks, and the outcome is a position adjustment. These are different projects.

issues.summary: The plan uses equal-weighted combination of linguistic families with separate elastic-net alternative that requires 'sign agreement and rank-correlation >0.7,' but does not explain what happens if the elastic-net weights give a different rank-order of observations.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan first computes evasiveness as the equal-weighted mean of five families, then separately fits elastic-net logistic weights. The robustness check requires 'sign agreement' (same direction of effect) and 'rank-correlation >0.7' (same rank order of firm-quarters). But rank-correlation >0.7 is a high bar for a predictor — a ρ=0.70 means 51% of the variance in ranks is shared (ρ²=0.49), which is respectable but not high. If the two methods give different rank-orders, which one is used? The plan does not say. If the elastic-net shows that some families have near-zero weight (e.g., 'length' is not informative), that finding should be incorporated, not relegated to a robustness check.
issues.what_breaks: H2 test and interpretability. If the elastic-net method gives meaningfully different weights (e.g., deflection: 0.6, hedging: 0.3, length: 0.05), that tells you which linguistic features matter. But if the plan uses equal-weighting as the primary and relegates elastic-net to 'sign agreement check,' the conclusion is based on a suboptimal model. If the models disagree on rank-correlation <0.7, the plan says this indicates a problem, but does not say what the problem is or how to fix it.
issues.fix: Either: (1) Use elastic-net throughout (fit on training set 2005–2016, apply to test set 2017–present, report weights). This buys you data-driven weighting without extra degrees of freedom. Or (2) Use equal-weighting as pre-registered primary and elastic-net as post-hoc robustness, but show the weights and discuss which linguistic features are carrying the signal (if 90% of elastic-net weight is on deflection, explain why). Do not require the two to agree in rank-correlation; instead, explain why they diverge if they do.

issues.summary: The plan does not state what happens if a company has multiple vendor renegotiations in the window (e.g., company A renegotiates contracts with three major suppliers in different quarters), making it unclear whether the ΔScore is specific to the renegotiation or a general state.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan measures ΔScore within a firm-quarter, comparing vendor-topic evasiveness to other topics and to baseline. But if a company has chronic vendor renegotiation (e.g., a low-margin business that is always pushing back on supplier terms), the ΔScore is elevated across many periods, not a signal of a specific deal going bad. The plan would tag many periods as 'vendor-specific evasiveness elevated' and would try to predict margin surprises in all of them, which is less clean than a clean single-event study.
issues.what_breaks: H1 and H2. If the sample includes chronic-renegotiation companies where ΔScore is always elevated, the signal is not 'this deal is hard,' it is 'this company is always negotiating.' The margin surprises in that company are not informative about the specific renegotiation; they are just general business conditions. This contaminates the regression.
issues.fix: Exclude or stratify: For each firm, count how many quarters have elevated ΔScore on vendor topics (using the 1.5 SD threshold). If a firm exceeds some threshold (e.g., >30% of quarters), exclude it as a chronic negotiator, or analyze it separately. This keeps the signal focused on *event-specific* evasiveness, not background noise.

issues.summary: The plan claims it will 'compute power beforehand' (mentioned in pitfalls) but does not show the calculation or the required sample size.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A power analysis requires an assumed effect size. The plan does not state: 'We expect a 1-SD increase in ΔScore to predict a 15bp margin surprise (effect size: ~Cohen's d = 0.2 for binary outcome), which with 40,000 observations gives power >0.95 to detect |t|≥2.5.' Without this calculation, the claim to have 'computed power' is unsubstantiated.
issues.what_breaks: Evidence standard. If the power calculation shows that the required sample size is 50,000 but the plan only has 40,000 effective observations (after droppage), the target |t|≥2.5 is over-ambitious.
issues.fix: Pre-spec: 'We have 40,000 firm-quarters. Assuming Prob(negative surprise) = 30%, and evasiveness increases this probability by 5pp (relative risk = 1.17), power to detect this at α=0.05 two-sided is [X]%. If power is <80%, the target threshold is not achievable and we will lower it to |t|≥2.0 or use a one-sided test.' Show the power curve.

issues.summary: The plan does not specify how to handle the case where a company does not renegotiate a vendor contract in a given year (no exchange occurs), which may itself be informative (lack of renegotiation = strong position = less margin risk).
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan requires '≥3 vendor exchanges and ≥150 words' and reports 'insufficient evidence' if these are not met. But absence of discussion is different from evasiveness in discussion. A company that does not mention vendors at all in a call might have a strong bargaining position (no need to renegotiate, terms are favorable), or it might be a company where vendor risk is not material (e.g., a software company with low COGS). The plan treats 'insufficient evidence' as a missing observation, but it could be an informative signal (no concern about vendors = low evasiveness score = should predict *positive* margin surprises).
issues.what_breaks: H1 measurement. If the plan drops firm-quarters with no vendor discussion, it is conditioning on firms that explicitly discuss vendors. This is selection bias: the sample is firms that are in negotiation or disclosure mode on vendors, not a representative cross-section. A company with strong vendor relationships might never discuss them (low evasiveness = low signal, but not because they are evasive, because they have nothing to discuss).
issues.fix: Create a three-level outcome: (a) Firm discusses vendors and evasiveness ≥1.5 SD = 'evasive,' (b) Firm discusses vendors and evasiveness <1.5 SD = 'not evasive,' (c) Firm does not discuss vendors = 'silent.' Test whether 'silent' firms have lower or higher margin surprises than 'not evasive' firms. If silent firms have margin surprises similar to 'not evasive,' the lack of discussion is uninformative. If silent firms have lower surprises (better margins), evasiveness is informative. Include this in the model: use a categorical variable (evasive / not evasive / silent) rather than a binary evasiveness score.

result.overall: This plan proposes using NLP-based evasiveness detection on earnings-call transcripts to predict margin surprises and establish a general mechanism (evasiveness as a signal). However, it is fundamentally mis-scoped for its audience: it was written for a systematic firm with 10+ analyst data-science infrastructure, but is being proposed to a concentrated long-only manager who makes few big bets and needs explainable, actionable calls on specific businesses. The plan mistakes a *capability-build* (can we measure evasiveness broadly and does it predict margins?) for a *single-name decision* (is this company's vendor risk underpriced?). The original question can be answered in 1–2 weeks via hand-audit of calls and filings; the proposed plan takes 4+ months and produces a cross-sectional signal that may not apply to this company at all. Additionally, the plan relies on infrastructure (production NLP pipelines, LLM inference, person-ID tracking, classifier validation) that this firm cannot operate without external partnership, and the results cannot be defended to an IC without simplification. Start with the cheap version: a hand-read of the company's calls around the renegotiation, a quick scan of Item 1A and competitor positioning, and a decision on whether the margin risk is priced. If successful, and if the firm's other positions trigger similar questions, *then* invest in building the signal infrastructure—but as a separate, explicitly-scoped capability project with its own timeline and staffing. As written, the plan burns resources without answering the question it was asked.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic quant shop with infrastructure to maintain panel data, run panel econometrics, and iterate through multiple specifications and validation cuts.
result.what_would_falsify: Refit on consumption-priced names shows equal performance; rolling-origin MAPE exceeds 150 bps or fails to beat carry-forward on Diebold–Mariano p<0.05 in rolling windows; systematic decays per-year check. No commitment to which of these ends the work.

issues.summary: The entire analysis pipeline — panel unit-root tests, cointegration, Driscoll–Kraay, wild cluster bootstrap, rolling-origin validation, splicing, Bai–Perron screening — cannot be executed or defended by a five-person shop with no engineers, no database, and no econometric software license.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan opens with CIPS and Westerlund tests, ECM estimation, and Pesaran CD — tests and estimators not available in Bloomberg or Excel. Driscoll–Kraay and wild cluster bootstrap are standard in Stata or R for panel shops; they do not exist in native Excel. The plan requires backfilled data structured as a balanced quarterly panel by company, point-in-time stamped, with splice rules applied across multiple vendor sources, spliced on overlap ratios, and screened for structural breaks — this is a SQL+git workflow, not a manual task. A single analyst running this in Excel would make splicing errors, lose data-lineage documentation, and have no way to audit coverage or missingness by company-quarter. The people receiving this cannot check the Pesaran CD cross-sectional dependence test or validate a Driscoll–Kraay lag selection, so it cannot carry a decision. The firm buys datasets occasionally but cannot maintain a backfilled historical panel; they buy research, they do not build research infrastructure.
issues.what_breaks: Every step downstream of data assembly. The analyst starts building a panel in October, gets halfway through three data sources in December, discovers Datos and Verto disagree on 12 companies in Q3 2021, then has to decide arbitrarily. CIPS test results come back; nobody knows what a p-value of 0.043 on the Pesaran test means for the next step. The model is fit, residuals cluster on a handful of names, rolling-origin code does not exist, and the chart of fitted vs. actual gets sent to the IC as the validation. The PM asks 'what beats carry-forward?' The analyst cannot say because Diebold–Mariano was never run. The plan dies three months in with nothing to show except a messy spreadsheet.
issues.fix: Strip the econometric armor. Specify: (A) One panel data source: pick Similarweb or Datos, commit beforehand, get one year of history backfilled by the vendor at purchase, and do not splice. (B) Estimation: OLS in log-log form, within company, no lags or unit-root tests — just levels and year-over-year differences, both shown, residuals inspected. (C) Validation: Holdout 20% by company; compare MAPE of the MAU model to carry-forward and four-quarter trend using hand-arithmetic, report the ratio in the sample. (D) One pre-committed falsifier: if the coefficient on log MAU flips negative or is smaller than 0.2 in any split, stop and report that instead of building further. That is a six-week version; if it works, hire infrastructure and do the real version later.

issues.summary: The plan conflates two different research questions — 'Does MAU predict the growth in ARR' (mechanism test, narrow) and 'Can we beat a statistical model that carries forward ARR with MAU as a predictor' (forecasting, broad) — and the evidence standard is built for the second while the question is the first.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The hypothesis states: within a company, 1% MAU → β% ARR one quarter or less, residuals smaller than sell-side dispersion. This is a mechanism claim: the billed unit (seats) should move with the used unit (MAU), with a stable elasticity. The validation then pivots to rolling-origin prediction of absolute ARR and competition with the carry-forward model using Diebold–Mariano. These are not the same test. A mechanism test on elasticity asks: does the coefficient on log MAU hold steady across splits, is the sign right, is magnitude plausible given pricing? A forecasting test asks: does this model predict future ARR better than alternatives? The plan builds a forecasting apparatus (rolling-origin, MAPE, Diebold–Mariano) when it should first establish the elasticity mechanism, then ask whether it is useful for prediction. If β = 0.6 but carry-forward beats the MAU model on rolling-origin because of trend dominance, the mechanism is real but the forecast is not useful — the plan treats this as failure of the whole hypothesis. Conversely, if MAU forecasts well only because it happens to be correlated with a multi-year trend the model captures via fixed effects, the mechanism is not established at all. The two conclusions are inverted and the validation is built to conflate them.
issues.what_breaks: The investment decision. The PM reads: 'MAU predicts ARR; beats carry-forward on rolling-origin p<0.05.' They think the mechanism is proven and MAU is a leading indicator they can use for modeling. It is neither. If the next quarter two names miss guidance badly, the PM discovers the rolling-origin performance was trend-capture, not MAU sensitivity. The plan has sold a forecasting result as a mechanism result and the firm buys it because the validation language ('claim survives', 'replication', 'beats benchmark') sounds rigorous. Six months later the edge is gone.
issues.fix: Choose one goal. If the goal is mechanism: drop rolling-origin validation entirely. Instead, show (1) the β coefficient from within-company estimation, (2) whether it is stable across (a) size quintiles, (b) three sub-periods, (c) positive and negative surprise regimes, (d) cloud vs. on-prem mix, (3) whether the elasticity is consistent with pricing moves (e.g., a 10% price increase with stable MAU should predict flat or falling ARR, and does it?), (4) the null is β not significantly different from zero or from a mechanical bound. If the goal is forecasting: keep rolling-origin validation but drop the elasticity claim, report the MAPE ratio, compare to an analyst-consensus benchmark (not carry-forward), and commit upfront that you will only trade if MAPE beats consensus by >50 bps in rolling windows *and* the advantage persists in the year following the training window.

issues.summary: The false-positive cost is concentrated and high (spotting MAU as a leading indicator when it is noise means allocating capital to timing bets on 35–60 names), but the error posture is built for the opposite regime.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This firm is concentrated, buys three to five year holding periods, and lives and dies by being right about the *business*. A false positive here is 'MAU moves faster than ARR, so we can model near-term outperformance by loading on MAU beats and lightening on MAU misses.' If MAU is actually lagging or coincident, not leading, this strategy will whipsaw — the firm adds on MAU dips that are early warnings the business is slowing, and sells on MAU spikes that are trailing indicators of growth already priced. That is a permanent edge destroyer, not a diversifiable mistake. The plan's posture is Bayesian accumulation: CIPS, Westerlund, Pesaran CD, wild cluster bootstrap, rolling-origin, Diebold–Mariano, Bai–Perron, falsification on consumption names — a belt-and-suspenders apparatus designed to avoid false positives. But the gate is still p<0.05, which in a panel of 900 company-quarters with 35–60 clusters is a low bar for spurious association. Multiple lags, two transformation choices (level and first-difference), company trends on or off, mobile included or excluded, price controls on or off — there are 32 specification combinations, all fitted. The plan does not correct for this; it 'chooses on rolling-origin performance', which is another way of mining. The multiple-comparison problem is buried.
issues.what_breaks: The model passes rolling-origin validation in-sample because the training window is rolling, so each test is a post-hoc comparison tuned to not over-fit *within its window*. But across the 12 rolling windows and 32 specs, the model that gets reported is the one that happened to work best on the last window. By the time the firm is ready to trade, the spec is fit, and the market will not wait for the spec that works even better in the next window. Simultaneously, out-of-sample here means 'held out from the training window'; it does not mean 'held out from the entire research process.' The choice to include price controls, the decision to spliceOn 0.9 overlap ratio instead of 0.85, the exclusion of consumption names from the main sample — all are pre-committed but informed by prior looks at the same data. A model that survives rolling-origin on one training window often fails on the next because the researcher chose the config that worked best in-sample on the first.
issues.fix: Commit beforehand to one specification: log-log, within company, one lag (ARR[t] ~ MAU[t-1] + company + quarter), no price controls, no mobile splits, no re-estimation in differences unless the level β is negative. Pre-commit the false-positive threshold: if the coefficient is between 0 and 0.3, or if it is not statistically different from zero at p<0.10 using *unadjusted* cluster-robust standard errors (not wild bootstrap, not Pesaran CD), stop and report the result as null rather than excavating for an alternate spec. Alternatively, pre-register the entire analysis in the SSRN registry or with the firm's compliance, including the 32 specifications, before fitting any data, and report all 32 results. Doing that will kill the false positive, because the p-hacking is visible.

issues.summary: The plan is written as a black-box forecasting pipeline (CIPS tests, ECM, Diebold–Mariano) when the firm is a handful of analysts without infrastructure to run it or people on the IC to evaluate it.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The firm's IC includes PMs trained in narrative fundamental analysis over decades. They can inspect a worked example — walk through one company, show the revenue bridge, MAU changes, check the elasticity math with a calculator, spot where pricing moved or churn crept up. They cannot evaluate a Driscoll–Kraay standard error or a Diebold–Mariano p-value in a wild cluster bootstrap. If the analyst says 'the model beats carry-forward, p<0.05', and the PM asks 'show me on three names,' the analyst will have to go back to the spreadsheet and generate that data — but it is not in the plan, so the analyst will do it wrong or produce anecdotes that do not match the aggregate result. The plan is built to optimize for aggregate statistical power across 900 company-quarters, which is the wrong optimization for this firm. A concentrated manager trades on conviction on specific names; the fact that a statistical model works in aggregate is irrelevant if it fails on the names in the portfolio. The tool cannot be explained after it is built, and that makes it unusable to the PM, so it cannot influence a decision even if the hypothesis is correct.
issues.what_breaks: The validation section. The plan says 'Claim survives only if the MAU model beats C out-of-sample under Diebold–Mariano on absolute-error differentials, clustered by quarter, p < 0.05'. The analyst runs the test, gets p=0.047, reports success to the IC. The PM asks: 'On which three companies does MAU most clearly predict quarterly growth, and by how much?' The analyst looks at residuals, picks the three with lowest MAPE, and shows them — but those may be the ones where carry-forward was also wrong, so MAU's win is accidental. Or the analyst shows the three largest coefficient values, but log-coefficients do not have an intuitive meaning for sizing positions. Nobody on the IC can evaluate whether 0.047 is a real effect or noise, because they do not know what the test means or whether three trailing quarters could have occurred by chance. The PM decides not to act because they cannot defend it to partners or compliance, and the analysis produces a report that nobody uses. That is not a defect in the research; it is a defect in fitting the research to the firm.
issues.fix: Restructure for a concentrated audience: (A) Pick the 8–12 largest names by AUM exposure in the firm's process (Salesforce, HubSpot, ServiceNow, Atlassian, Asana, etc.). (B) For each, show the ARR path, MAU path, and elasticity by hand over the past 12 quarters. Plot both series. (C) State the predicted elasticity: if MAU is up 20% and price flat, what does the model predict for ARR? What actually happened? (D) Across the set, calculate: 'In how many quarters did MAU move before ARR moved in the same direction, and by what lag?' (E) Report as yes/no: Is the lag zero to one quarter, or is it longer? If longer, the model is not useful for tactical positioning. (F) Report the dispersion: Is the elasticity 0.4 for half the names and 0.8 for the other half? If so, it is not a reliable signal. Do this for the 8–12 names by hand, present the table to the IC, and let them see the data. That is the validation this firm can use; it is also cheaper and faster.

issues.summary: The panel data construction is complex, sourced from multiple vendors with rules for splicing and screening that cannot be audited by non-engineers and that will leak researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan pulls from Similarweb, Datos, Verto, Sensor Tower, and Visible Alpha. It splices on an overlap ratio or truncates pre-break history after Bai–Perron screening. It excludes companies where the authenticated hostname cannot be confirmed or where mobile/app split is material. It flags disagreement between two sources, but does not say how big a disagreement triggers exclusion. It includes 35–60 names with 'rule fixed beforehand: seat-metered >70%', but that is a judgment call per 10-K — two analysts could disagree on whether Salesforce or Workday is 70% subscription revenue. A single analyst at this firm will read three 10-Ks, decide on seat-metering differently than the person who audits the work, and nobody will notice until the model is published. The Bai–Perron test on log levels for tracker re-basings is correctly motivated but the threshold for 'step change' is not stated. Is a 10% jump automatic drop? 5%? The plan says 'cross-check vendor notes, splice on an overlap ratio or drop pre-break history' — but that is three different choices and the analyst will pick the one that keeps the most data or produces the nicest fitted line. No version control, no data lineage, no ability to reproduce.
issues.what_breaks: Six months after the publication, a journalist or a short-seller notices that the firm has excluded Q2 2019 for Asana because of a 're-basing', but internal research records show Asana did not change vendors then — it was just a discontinuity in the Similarweb data. The data was dropped to fit the model better, not because it was invalid. The firm cannot defend the exclusion, because there is no git log showing why the decision was made. The core inference is now suspect: did the model work because of the mechanism, or because of the splicing? This is not paranoia; it is what happened to multiple published cross-sectional studies in finance when datasets were made public and audited.
issues.fix: Use one data vendor only. Commit: 'We will source MAU from Similarweb, which provides monthly uniques at the app level. We require a minimum of 20 monthly observations per company. We will not splice or backfill; we will begin the analysis with the first month both Similarweb and ARR data exist for that company, and we will end with the most recent month available. We will not screen on Bai–Perron or any other structural break test; instead, we will flag quarters within two months of announced changes (new pricing, acquisition of a major competitor, major customer win/loss) and will show results both with and without those quarters. We will use the 'with' results as the headline.' That loses the longer history and some statistical power, but it is defensible and reproducible. The sample becomes smaller and less elegant; the analysis becomes trustworthy.

issues.summary: The plan gates the conclusion on a falsification test ('refit on consumption-priced names; equal performance sinks the thesis') but does not specify what 'equal performance' means, so the result will be rationalized no matter what.
issues.why_it_applies_here: 'Equal performance sinks the thesis' — but equal in what metric? MAPE? Rolling-origin Diebold–Mariano? Coefficient sign? At what threshold does the model count as having 'failed' the falsification? If the MAU model on Snowflake and Datadog has MAPE of 12% vs. 10% on the seat-priced names, that is clearly worse, so the thesis holds — but if it is 10.5% vs. 10%, is that 'equal'? The plan does not say. The analyst will compute the test, see 10.5%, declare it sufficiently higher than 10%, report that consumption names behave differently (validating the hypothesis), and move on. Or the analyst will compute it and find that the consumption-priced names have higher volatility, smaller N, and a noisier result, so the MAPE is actually higher but the coefficient is also higher and in the right direction, so conclude that the underlying mechanism is the same but the measurement is worse. The falsification is toothless because the criterion is not specified in advance.
issues.what_breaks: The validation section. The plan promises: 'Falsification: refit on the excluded consumption-priced names; equal performance sinks the thesis.' The analyst refits the model on Snowflake, Datadog, MongoDB, and Confluent (consumption-metered). The coefficient on log MAU is positive and 0.35, vs. 0.55 for the seat-metered sample. The error is 11.2% vs. 10%. Is that equal? The analyst can argue it both ways: (1) 'The coefficient is 35% lower and the error is 10% higher, which shows the mechanism is different — seats drive ARR tighter than consumption, as predicted.' (2) 'The mechanism still works; consumption pricing is just noisier because of churn and usage volatility, so the MAU signal is weaker but present.' Both arguments are plausible and the thesis survives either interpretation. The falsification does not falsify.
issues.fix: Pre-commit a numerical threshold: 'Falsification: refit the model on consumption-metered names. If the coefficient on log MAU is below 0.3 in absolute value, or if rolling-origin MAPE on consumption names is more than 150 bps higher than on seat-metered names, we will report the hypothesis as unsupported for the consumption segment and restrict all subsequent trading to seat-metered names only.' Specify direction and magnitude in advance. Or do not do a falsification test; instead, report the coefficients and errors separately by pricing model and let the IC decide whether the pattern makes sense. That is more honest.

issues.summary: The plan claims it will identify per-seat vendors by >70% subscription-revenue rule, then exclude based on vendor-level judgment calls (authentication hostname, material mobile usage) with no pre-committed criteria.
issues.why_it_applies_here: 'Rule fixed beforehand: seat-metered >70% of subscription revenue per 10-K or management' — but management sometimes cites subscription revenue differently in guidance vs. the 10-K, especially for companies that have acquired other businesses. Salesforce, for instance, had a large professional-services arm for years; is that subscription revenue? HubSpot and Zendesk both have professional-services and managed services; should those be stripped? The 70% rule is a reasonable heuristic but it is not objective. 'Authenticated hostnames only (app.*, *.my.*, wildcard tenant subdomains), never marketing www; confirm wildcard rollup.' — This excludes companies that use www.company.com for login or a third-party auth provider. Slack, for example, is accessed via direct web links and workspace subdomains, not app.slack.com. Is Slack in or out? The plan says to 'confirm wildcard rollup', but who confirms it? An analyst reading Similarweb documentation? That will produce different results from a vendor support query. 'Enterprise SSO under-panelling versus SMB, deep-link misattribution, bots, moving desktop/mobile split; include app MAU or restrict to immaterial-mobile names, held fixed.' — This is a Pandora's box of potential confounders, and the plan says 'include app MAU or restrict to immaterial-mobile names'. Those are two different analyses and the choice will be made ex-post on which looks better. The rules are not fixed; they are guidelines for judgment calls.
issues.what_breaks: Company inclusion. The analyst includes HubSpot (marketing automation + CRM, professional services material), excludes ZoomInfo (similar, but the analyst thinks the services portion is higher), and includes Zendesk (support platform, some professional services but less). The three are not comparable on the dimension the model assumes (seat-metering), and the model is fit on a heterogeneous set. When the results are published, a peer questions why HubSpot is in the sample at all given its consulting revenue, and the analyst cannot point to a rule — it is a judgment call made months ago in a spreadsheet. The reputational damage is small but the inference is now suspect.
issues.fix: Specify the rule in advance: 'Subscription revenue is defined as recurring annual revenue from software licensing as stated in the firm's 10-K Note on Revenue Recognition. Professional services, implementation, and support contracts billed as separate line items are excluded. We define seat-metered as follows: the company must explicitly state or report that ARR scales with the number of authorized users or seats. We will use the most recent 10-K and one follow-up call transcript. If either source states seat-metering, the company is included. We will apply this rule to all 35–60 candidate names and publish the classification before fitting any model.' Then do it and stick to it. Or: use a third-party classification (a vendor like SimilarWeb that already categorizes business model) and commit to that classification. That removes the judgment and the researcher degrees of freedom.

issues.summary: The plan promises to measure β as 0.4–0.8 and to validate against sell-side dispersion, but neither the prediction nor the benchmark is pre-committed in units a PM can understand.
issues.why_it_applies_here: 'Expect β 0.4–0.8' — this is stated as the hypothesis. But a log-log coefficient of 0.6 means a 10% increase in MAU predicts a 6% increase in ARR in the next quarter or less. Is that useful for positioning? The plan does not say. 'Residuals smaller than sell-side dispersion' — sell-side dispersion in what? Quarterly subscription revenue growth? Annual ARR? The plan does not specify. 'Consensus from Visible Alpha line items (subscription revenue, ARR, NRR, billings) at print morning, with contributor count and cross-analyst standard deviation' — this is data collection, not a specified benchmark. When the analysis is done, the plan says 'In growth terms: median absolute year-over-year error below 150 bps and below cross-analyst consensus dispersion in ≥60% of company-quarters.' So the bar is the lower of (1) 150 bps absolute error, and (2) the cross-analyst dispersion on that company's ARR. For Salesforce, consensus dispersion is probably ±3–4% (very tight); for smaller names, it might be ±8–10%. The model might beat (2) for all names without ever reaching (1), so the success criterion is different for different names. That is not a weakness if it is pre-stated and justified (analyst disagreement *is* a useful yardstick for model error), but it is not pre-stated here — it is a rationalization waiting to happen.
issues.what_breaks: Validation and signaling. The analyst trains the model, runs the test, and finds median absolute YoY error of 160 bps on seat-metered names. That misses the 150 bps bar, so the model 'fails' the first criterion. But the median consensus dispersion is 140 bps, and the model beats that in 68% of company-quarters, so the analyst reports success on the second criterion. The IC reads the publication and believes the model beats analyst consensus, which is a strong claim. Three months later, the model fails on an out-of-time test set (because the model was fit to the dispersion metric, which is high when volatility is high, so the model is biased toward volatile periods), and the claim is revealed as an artifact of the validation criterion. Had the criterion been pre-specified, the analyst could not have cherry-picked it.
issues.fix: Pre-commit one success metric: either (1) absolute error below 150 bps, or (2) outperforms consensus dispersion in >60% of quarters, or (3) Diebold–Mariano p<0.05 vs. carry-forward. Pick one, not multiple, and state it in the pre-committed plan. If the model fails, it fails; do not report it as a qualified success. Alternatively, use the simplest test: 'The model will be considered validated if, in a rolling-origin setup (train through T, predict T+1, repeat for last 12 quarters), the prediction error is lower than the consensus dispersion on 7 or more of the 12 quarters.' That is hard to game and a PM can understand it immediately.

issues.summary: The plan requires panel econometrics (CIPS, Westerlund, Driscoll–Kraay, wild cluster bootstrap, Pesaran CD), specification searches (32 combinations), and bespoke data assembly that cannot be executed in Excel and cannot be explained to the IC without a technical appendix they will not read.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The simplest hypothesis is: within a company, when MAU goes up, does ARR grow faster? The simplest test is: for each company, regress ∆ARR on ∆MAU over time, look at the distribution of the 35–60 individual regression slopes, and ask whether most are positive and significant. That is a 30-minute Excel analysis. Instead, the plan proposes a pooled panel with company fixed effects, two alternative lag structures, first-difference and ECM forms, unit-root tests, cointegration tests, wild cluster bootstrap, and multiple validation cuts. Why? The stated reason is to ensure the relationship is not spurious (unit root in both series). The actual reason is the analyst is trained in panel econometrics and it is the obvious path once you have a balanced panel. But the firm does not have panel econometrics software or people who understand the output, and the PM does not need the extra power: they only care whether the signal is real on the names they own. The plan has imported a quant methodology where a fundamental methodology would be more credible.
issues.what_breaks: Execution and trust. The analyst spends four weeks building the panel, two weeks running CIPS tests and interpreting Pesaran CD, one week debugging the Driscoll–Kraay implementation, and one week on rolling-origin validation. When the analysis is finished, the PM asks 'does this work?' The analyst says 'yes, the coefficient is 0.58 and significant at the 5% level using wild cluster bootstrap.' The PM cannot evaluate that, so they ask for three examples. The analyst shows Salesforce: MAU up 5%, ARR up 3%. HubSpot: MAU up 8%, ARR up 4%. Asana: MAU down 2%, ARR down 1%. The PM looks at the numbers and thinks 'this is not robust to me', because two of the three show elasticity lower than the pooled estimate and one is half the predicted elasticity. The PM decides not to trade because they cannot defend it to others, and the eight weeks of work produces a report with a bottom-line conclusion they do not believe. Meanwhile, a simple by-name analysis would have shown the PM the same heterogeneity upfront and they could have decided to trade on the subset where elasticity is strongest.
issues.fix: Start with the simplest analysis: (1) For each of the 8–12 core names, estimate ARR change on MAU change by hand over the past 12 quarters. Plot both series on the same chart. (2) Calculate the correlation between ∆log(ARR) and ∆log(MAU) for each name, and report the median across names. (3) Note the lag: in how many quarters does MAU move first, and in how many do they move together? (4) If the median elasticity is positive and the lag is ≤1 quarter, the hypothesis is provisionally supported. If not, stop. (5) Only if this works, pool the 8–12 names and run OLS with company dummies to estimate the average elasticity and check whether it holds across all names simultaneously. Report both the individual slopes and the pooled estimate; let the PM see both. This is a one-week analysis, produces outputs the PM can understand and defend, and either kills the idea or gives it enough credibility to take forward. The panel econometrics can come later if the firm hires an engineer.

issues.summary: The plan does not specify what an analyst and PM would actually do with the output. Is the model used to forecast ARR for valuation? To time exits? To identify mispriced growth? The intended use case is absent, which means the evidence standard and required confidence are uncalibrated.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The research question is 'Do MAU lead ARR?', which is a mechanistic question, not an investment question. A PM cares about the answer only if it changes a position decision: e.g., 'If MAU growth slows, we reduce our AUM allocation to this name; if it accelerates, we add.' That requires: (1) a consistent lead time so you have notice before ARR disappoints, (2) enough volatility in the signal that it matters for quarterly earnings estimates, (3) low false-positive rate because each false positive costs real money on a concentrated portfolio. The plan does not state any of these. Is the model meant for quarterly earnings forecasting (compare to consensus), or for multi-year valuation (capture the slope of the power-law of seats and monetization)? Is it meant to be a sell signal (to get out before the quarter when growth slows) or a buy signal (to identify recovery)? Is it meant to cover all 35–60 names or a subset? Without the intended use case, the precision bar is unknown. A forecasting model for quarterly earnings needs sub-quarter accuracy because the earnings surprise is what moves stock. A model for multi-year ARR trends can afford error in that range because the trend is stable. The plan conflates both.
issues.what_breaks: Sizing and the IC decision. The analyst finishes the research and presents: 'MAU leads ARR by one quarter with elasticity 0.55.' The PM asks: 'How much capital should I allocate to this signal?' The analyst has no answer, because the research question was whether the signal exists, not how much money to make from it. The analyst has to go back and estimate the number of quarterly surprises the signal could catch, how large they are, and what the P&L would be on a position sized to that. That is a second research project. Or the PM asks: 'On which quarters would this have failed us?' The analyst looks back and finds two years (2019–2021) where MAU beat but ARR missed anyway — was that sample selection or is the signal only good in some regimes? Again, a second analysis. The original research produces a neat finding but no actionable implication, so it gets published on the internal research board and forgotten.
issues.fix: Specify the intended use case: (A) 'We will use this to forecast the next quarter's subscription revenue relative to consensus. If MAU is up X% YoY and consensus is up Y%, we will adjust our earnings model by [(0.55 × X) − Y] percent. We will trade on this adjustment only if it is ≥100 bps in the growth rate.' (B) 'We will monitor MAU monthly via Similarweb. When MAU growth falls below a three-month moving average minus one standard deviation for a given name, we will reduce our allocation by 10% as a hedge against a near-term ARR miss. When it jumps by ≥15% YoY, we will increase by 5%.' (C) 'We will use MAU as a confirmatory indicator for our multi-year TAM and unit economics thesis. If MAU stalls, we will revisit our assumed growth rate; if it accelerates, we will stress-test our dilution assumptions.' Pick one, size the analysis to answer it, and plan the validation accordingly.

issues.summary: No alternative hypothesis or mechanism is developed. The plan assumes MAU should lead ARR for per-seat vendors but does not engage with the possibility that price-mix (sales price per seat) drifts faster than MAU, or that the model is finding ARR's own momentum under a different variable name.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The hypothesis statement says 'the mechanism needs MAU-per-seat and price per seat drifting slowly'. This is stated but not tested. The plan includes a price control (Wayback snapshots of pricing pages), but the pricing index is ad-hoc and likely incomplete. Salesforce and HubSpot change their pricing every few years and also bundle SKUs, so the snapshot price does not capture mix shift. The plan's response is 'else flag and exclude quarters after announced increases', which is giving up on the quarters where the signal is most likely to be useful. Meanwhile, the alternative hypothesis — that ARR is driven by pricing and mix, not seat growth, but the model picks up the signal because MAU and prices both trend up — is never tested. For instance: if a company raises price 10% in Q1 and MAU is flat, the model predicts ARR up 0% (because β=0.55 and MAU up 0%), but ARR is actually up 10%, so the model fails. But if the price increase happened three months before the MAU measurement, the effect is back-loaded into the next quarter. The model would look like it is working when it is just capturing the tail of an announced price action. The plan tries to control for this ('log price actions from Wayback pricing-page snapshots as a log price index control'), but the control is weak because Wayback snapshots are not contemporaneous with implementation and do not capture discounting. A stronger test would be: 'We will exclude all quarters within two quarters of an announced price change, refit the model, and report whether β holds. If it does not, the mechanism is driven by price, not seats.'
issues.what_breaks: The interpretation. The model fits, the coefficient is positive, and the validation passes. The PM believes MAU leads ARR. Then Salesforce does a surprise price increase and guidance beat even though MAU was flat, and the PM realizes the model had been capturing a different signal: mix and pricing. The firm has not been timing based on seat growth; they have been timing based on a stale price index. The next cycle, this breaks.
issues.fix: Test the alternative: (1) Refit the model excluding all quarters with ±2 of an announced price or product bundle change. If the coefficient on MAU changes by >20% or loses significance, the price mechanism is important and should be modeled separately. (2) Build a price index from company filings (extracted from Note 1, revenue recognition policy) or earnings calls (CFO guidance on price increase rationale). Do not use Wayback; it is too backward-looking. (3) Regress ARR on (∆log(MAU), ∆log(price_index), ∆log(seats)) separately for companies where you can construct seat numbers from employment (e.g., Workday, Paycom). If seats have a different coefficient than MAU in those names, the MAU signal is not measuring seats; it is measuring something else. Do that analysis for three names by hand before scaling the model; it will either kill the hypothesis or strengthen it.

issues.summary: The plan requires MAU data sourced from four separate vendors, with criteria for splicing, exclusion, and validation that are not objectively specified and will produce different results if a different analyst executes them.
issues.why_it_applies_here: 'MAU from distinct-user panels (Similarweb app-level uniques, Datos, Verto, Sensor Tower/data.ai where app usage is material), preferring exposed monthly panel size; two sources where available, disagreement flagging quality.' — This is a procedural guideline, not a rule. For Asana, Similarweb and Datos disagree in 2021 Q2 by 15%. What does 'disagreement flagging quality' mean? Do both get excluded? Do we average them? Do we use the one with better absolute levels? The plan does not say. 'Authenticated hostnames only (app.*, *.my.*, wildcard tenant subdomains), never marketing www; confirm wildcard rollup.' — Salesforce is accessed via login.salesforce.com (not app.*). Does it qualify? HubSpot uses hubspotstarter.com and custom-branded login pages. The rule as stated would exclude both. But they are seat-metered providers and their inclusion is theoretically justified. The rule is too narrow, and the analyst will relax it. 'Preferring exposed monthly panel size' — Similarweb publishes a 'panel size' metric; smaller panel sizes (e.g., 10,000 monthly uniques instead of 100,000) create more noise. Prefer higher panel size, sure, but what is the cutoff? <5K uniques excluded? <10K? That changes the sample composition.
issues.what_breaks: Reproducibility. Six months later, a new analyst tries to update the analysis with newer data. They follow the rule as written and get a different sample (e.g., excluding Salesforce because it does not use app.*). They refit the model and get a different β. Was the hypothesis robust, or was the finding sample-specific? Now there is no way to know. Internal replication failed because the rules were not specified precisely enough.
issues.fix: Create a Classification Appendix before fitting any model: (1) For each of the 35–60 candidate names, list which vendor(s) the MAU data come from. (2) For each vendor, publish the credential for inclusion: 'We use Similarweb if the company has a mobile app and panel size ≥8,000 monthly uniques in ≥80% of observations. We use Datos if Similarweb is unavailable and panel size ≥5,000. We do not backfill between vendors; we use the earliest available source and continue with it.' (3) For each name, publish the authentication method used (app.*, *.my.*, www, etc.) and confirm that it captures the majority of user sessions. (4) If two sources disagree by >10% in any month, we flag that month and exclude it from the analysis, and note the exclusion in the results.' (5) Publish the Classification Appendix before fitting the model. This removes the flexibility and makes replication possible.

issues.summary: The plan does not specify when the analysis can be stopped early if the hypothesis is falsified, and it locks in a nine-week timeline regardless of what the first two weeks reveal.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The data assembly alone (pulling MAU from four sources, splicing, screening for breaks, confirming hostnames, assembling the ARR series from three sources and splicing) is estimated as four weeks. Only after that can the analysis begin. If the MAU data are too noisy (Similarweb sample sizes are 5K monthly uniques on average, which is not enough to measure the signal), the whole plan fails. But that is not discovered until week 5. If the company-level correlation between ∆log(MAU) and ∆log(ARR) is 0.1 (very weak), the signal is too faint for the pooled model to pick up, and the eight-week effort is wasted on specification search. But that is not discovered until week 6. The plan sequences the work as: (1) data (weeks 1–4), (2) unit-root tests (week 5), (3) model fit (week 6), (4) validation (weeks 7–8), (5) writing (week 9). None of this is adaptive. A cheaper version would be: (1) pull MAU and ARR for the 12 largest names (2 days), (2) plot the two series side by side and visually assess whether the lag and magnitude look right (1 day), (3) run simple OLS by name (1 day), (4) if the median elasticity is >0.3 and lag is ≤1 quarter, then assemble the full panel and fit the pooled model (3 weeks); else stop (4 days total).
issues.what_breaks: Resource allocation. The analyst starts the data assembly in October, finishes in November, runs CIPS tests in early December, and finds that the unit-root test says the series is non-stationary but the first-difference form shows no lag, which is technically contradictory and requires investigation. By mid-January, the analyst has not yet fit a model that makes sense. The PM asks for a preliminary finding in early February; there is none, because the plan did not front-load the kill criterion. Meanwhile, a competitive analysis using simple within-company OLS on the same 12 core names could have been published in mid-November with a clear yes/no answer, and the IC would have had time to act on it.
