The plan reads as a pitch to build a case for one stock, not as a reproducible signal the firm's infrastructure was built to operationalize.
issues.what_breaks: The entire output path breaks. Even if the analysis is right, it produces a single-name call (buy this company because RPO unrecognized, LTA durable, not priced). A systematic firm either needs: (1) a rule that classifies any company in a shortage-guidance event the same way, allowing parallel processing and replication, or (2) a confession that this is not a systematic trade—it is a special-situation call that belongs in a fundamental pod, not a quant research plan. The firm cannot staff both, so this either goes into the wrong org or gets built twice.
issues.fix: Reframe as: does shortage guidance, combined with the RPO/LTA framework, predict equity outperformance at *event-window* or *quarterly-return* frequency across a cohort of 30+ prior shortage episodes (memory/passives 2017–18, semis 2021–22, etc.)? That is a systematic question. If the answer is yes only for one name because that name is special, acknowledge it and route it to fundamental research, not as a quant signal. If the answer is that the effect works broadly, produce the rule, backtest it at the firm's trading horizon (days-to-weeks returns, transaction-cost-inclusive), and measure capacity. Do not produce both at once; pick one.

issues.summary: The method—tiered haircuts calibrated from prior shortage episodes, custom agreement scoring, coherence checks—is far too opaque and manual for a research committee to re-run, evaluate, or defend independently.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This firm has a stated production research platform designed to replicate any result before it trades. A method that depends on reading transcripts adversarially, scoring agreements on six semantic attributes, calibrating haircuts from prior cycles with judgment calls on 'worse company history', and reconstructing definitions is not replicable by an independent team. The haircuts (Tier 1 90–95%, Tier 2 70%, Tier 3 25–35%) are stated as if calibrated from data, but the plan does not say how—what company histories, which quarters, how many, error bounds. If those are judgment, say so. If they are data-driven, produce the prior-cycle methodology so the committee can verify it and spot if it has embedded look-ahead.
issues.what_breaks: The research committee will push back on the haircuts in the first meeting. They cannot defend them independently, so they cannot take the position to a trader. The proposal becomes a delay, not a green light.
issues.fix: Either: (1) produce a purely automated pipeline—parse 10-Ks for RPO via regex, use SEC-extracted data where it exists, replace agreement scoring with a text-model classifier built on a labelled corpus, and show that pipeline is robust; or (2) acknowledge the method is manual and route it as a one-off fundamental call, not a replicable signal. A hybrid (mostly automated, senior analyst hand-checks 5–10 key agreements per company as a calibration check) is defensible if you name what the hand-check is doing and why it matters.

issues.summary: A three-month execution plan to build a ten-year dataset, rebuild accounting, score agreements, backtest scenarios, and construct DCFs is scheduled as if the early kill-criterion work has been done; it has not.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan's thresholds and falsifiers are all conditional on building the full dataset and agreement register first. Before doing that work, the plan owes: (1) a check that RPO and announced LTA data are actually available in comparable form across the cohort (take five companies, spend two days, assess collection cost); (2) a backtest on *prior* shortage cycles using *only* public document counts and simple heuristics (e.g., count 8-Ks mentioning LTA in the shortage period, compare to forward returns) to see if the signal is even *there* before engineering it. If the public signal is too weak to see raw, the engineered version will not be robust. If data is missing or definitions fragmented, the entire three-month build is sunk cost before the idea is tested. Kill this first.
issues.what_breaks: The plan commits weeks of work (custom data pipeline, agreement scoring, scenario modelling) before asking whether the raw components even exist or correlate with future stock moves. If the data is messy, fragmented by company or era, or if the raw signal (shortage guidance → forward returns) is not there even before haircuts, the whole effort was wasted.
issues.fix: Front-load a two-week kill test: (1) Pull all 8-Ks, transcripts, 10-Qs for 5–7 shortage-guidance events from prior cycles (pick diverse: semis 2021, memory 2017, telecom 2000). (2) Extract RPO as reported in each 10-Q. Do it by hand. How long does it take? Does the data format change over time? Are there companies where RPO is not disclosed? (3) Manually tag LTAs mentioned in transcripts and 8-Ks. Do the count and dollar value rise during shortage periods? (4) Crude sort: quarters where guidance mentions shortage + RPO disclosed = potential signal. Backtest: do those stock prices outperform peers in the next 90 days, net of transaction costs? At what frequency? If the answer is no, or 'only for 1 in 7 companies,' or 'requires 6-month hold,' acknowledge it and stop. If yes, proceed to engineering the measurement. Budget: $8–12k, two weeks of one senior analyst's time. Final output: a data-availability scorecard and a raw-signal backtest showing whether there is anything to measure before measurement is engineered.

issues.summary: The threshold logic (all six conditions must hold) is so restrictive that it will disqualify plausible shortages, rebranding data as 'not a signal' when the underlying effect might still be there but heterogeneous.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A systematic firm profits from effects that hold *most of the time*, not *all conditions met*. The plan gates on six conditions: ≥60% NTM revenue in Tier 1/2 *and* ≥40% year-two coverage *and* cash ≥15% *and* top-3 share <45% *and* mirror ≥50% *and* horizon >2yr vs. implied. Failing any one = no signal. A company in a genuine shortage with 55% Tier 1/2 (not 60%), or 15% cash support (not 15%—the boundary case), gets binned as 'not constructive'. That is a threshold test, not a signal. For systematic trading with Type II dominance, this is backwards: set a *scoring rule* where each condition weighted by its predictive power, then backtest the score (0–100) against returns. A 55% Tier 1/2 with strong cash support might score 72 and still trade, while a 65% with no cash might score 48. The current logic invents a cliff where none exists in the data.
issues.what_breaks: The backtest will show that the six-conditions-AND logic rejects 60–70% of plausible shortage events, including some where returns are positive. The thresholds were chosen because they 'feel' tight, not because they were tested on prior data. The model then appears to underpredict power rather than to work well.
issues.fix: Run the backtest without thresholds first: score each prior shortage episode 0–100 based on the six factors. Backtest score vs. returns. Find the score that maximizes Sharpe and minimizes false negatives. That becomes your threshold. If the data show a hard cliff (score >70 → +3% return, score <70 → 0%), use AND logic. If it is a smooth slope, use the score. Report the trade-off: tighter threshold = fewer false positives, lower capacity; looser = more capacity, more noise. Let the trader choose.

issues.summary: The model asks 'what is EV not priced in?' by computing haircut-adjusted committed revenue and reverse-DCFing the market EV. But EV already reflects all public data and analyst models; showing that committed revenue is larger than the model does not prove market is wrong, only that your model is different.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan says 'current EV does not already price that.' How do you know? The 20 analysts covering this stock have looked at RPO, read 8-Ks, and estimated LTA backlog. They may have guessed the haircuts differently (used 50% instead of 70% for Tier 2), or assumed faster conversion, or modeled a different terminal margin. If the stock is already expensive, it may be because they see the same durability and priced it in. The plan has no statement of what consensus LTA/RPO assumption is, or buy-side positioning on the durability question. Is the stock already rallied post-guidance? Does the derivatives market price in upside? Are long-dated calls bid? These are not certainties they agree; they are questions that determine whether a better measurement is an edge or a restatement of consensus.
issues.what_breaks: If buy-side and sell-side have already tagged backlog up and priced the stock, your 'better' haircuts shift the price negligibly. You cannot know this without a pre-analysis positioning check.
issues.fix: Before building the model: (1) Collect consensus estimate for NTM revenue growth. (2) Reverse-DCF the current stock price using a mid-market cost of capital. Back out the implied LTA/backlog assumption in the consensus model. (3) Interview 3–4 sell-side analysts directly: do they model backlog conversion? What haircut do they use for non-cash LTAs? How much of the short-term guidance do they assume is already 'baked in'? (4) Check positioning: are long-dated calls rich vs. historical vol? Are hedge funds short or long this name on the LTA thesis? If consensus is already 70% of your haircuts and has LTA embedded, you have no edge; reframe as a validation study ('we confirm the durability thesis with better data') or stop. If consensus is at 40% haircut and you have a fundamental reason it should be 65%, you have an edge. State which is true before running the DCF.

issues.summary: The plan models three resolution scenarios (early, on-guidance, late) with 'full paths' (pricing rolloff, pushout exercise, inventory air-pocket) but does not say what probability to assign to each, how sensitive the equity return is to the branch taken, or which branch the market is currently pricing in.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A systematic trader needs to know: (1) what is the base case? (2) what is the bull/bear? (3) which branch is most likely? (4) how much of the return is in the base case vs. tail realized upside? The plan does not separate these. If 80% of the return is in the 'on guidance' case, and the market assigns 70% probability, the expected value is modest. If return is lumpy and concentrated in low-probability 'early recovery with pricing hold' case, the position is a lottery. A systematic trader needs to size against realized vol and probability-weighted return, not against the absolute spread of a scenario tree.
issues.what_breaks: The analyst will build the three cases, show that bull is worth +15%, bear is worth -8%, base is +3%, and stop there. A trader sees 15% upside but does not know if it is 5% or 50% probable. Size is wrong either way.
issues.fix: For each of the three resolution cases, assign a probability (even if rough: 'early recovery 20%, on-guide 50%, late 30%'). Compute prob-weighted return. Compare to the realized vol of the name and the market-implied move. If prob × return is <1% annualized alpha, the signal is not robust enough to trade at the firm's size. If it is 2–3%, size it and go. This also forces a check: 'does the market price early vs. late differently?' (e.g., do options show skew?). If they do, the market is already differentiated and your edge is narrower than the scenario range.

issues.summary: The plan does not state what result would make you abandon the shortage-to-durability link, other than mechanical filter failures (inventory, definition change). It has no pre-committed test of the *economic* hypothesis.
issues.why_it_applies_here: If you backtest and find: (1) shortage guidance + high haircut-adjusted committed revenue predicts 0% return; (2) companies do recover but at the same revenue growth rate as peers (no durable uplift); (3) prices immediately on RPO guidance and revert after realization—any of these kills the thesis. The plan does not pre-commit to what number would count as 'no effect' or 'mechanism is broken'. Without that, every outcome gets rationalized: 'the market was ahead of us', 'this company was special', 'our haircuts were conservative'. A backtest is not falsification without a pre-committed criterion.
issues.what_breaks: The research committee will ask: what result would make you say this does not work? If the answer is 'well, it depends', they will not clear the trade.
issues.fix: State a pre-committed backtest criterion: 'If companies with >70% haircut-adjusted Tier 1/2 committed revenue underperform peers by >5% annualized over the next 2 years, or show zero cumulative return vs. S&P 500 during the shortage period + 12 months, the hypothesis is false and the position is off.' Make it specific and testable *before* the backtest runs. Report the result against that criterion, not against a narrative.

issues.summary: The plan builds a ten-year intraday dataset, a quarterly forward revenue bridge, an agreement register with six-attribute scoring, three scenario DCFs, and a reverse-DCF calibration—all for one name. Cost: 6–8 weeks of senior analyst time, plus data fees. Expected output: a single-name buy/sell call.
issues.why_it_applies_here: This firm can build a ten-year intraday dataset in a quarter because it applies to thousands of tickers, spreads the cost, and operationalizes the infrastructure. Building the same for one name is not proportionate. A concentrated fundamental manager (AUM ~$100M, portfolio 30–50 names) would justify this effort on a single large position. A systematic firm trading $1B+ across 3,000+ instruments does not deploy analyst-quarters on single-name archaeology unless the signal is proven to work at scale first (see sequencing issue above).
issues.what_breaks: The analyst spends two months building a perfect model of one name. At the end, they discover the effect does not work because: (1) the market already priced it, (2) the company has an exception to the rule, or (3) the sample size in the backtest is too small to be confident. The time spent cannot be recovered or reused.
issues.fix: Prove the signal works at scale before optimizing for one name. Backtest on the 20–30 prior shortage episodes using automated/scalable methods. If the signal is there (Sharpe >0.5 gross, >0.3 net of costs), then invest in the single-name deep dive on the highest-conviction opportunity. If not, the deep dive is misdirected.

issues.summary: The plan does not clearly separate what is being tested (does shortage guidance predict revenue durability?) from what is being measured (how durable is it, and by how much?). As a result, it is unclear whether this is a hypothesis test with a binary yes/no, or an estimation problem where the answer is 'durability is X years, current pricing implies Y, upside is Z%'.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A systematic trader needs a clean binary or score: does this factor predict returns? For a single-name special-situation call, the question is 'is the company mispriced and by how much?' The plan conflates them. It reads parts as 'we are testing if the shortage-to-LTA link is real' (a hypothesis) and parts as 'we are modeling what the revenue duration should be' (an estimation/pricing question). The two have different evidence standards, horizons, and uses. A hypothesis test fails if p > 0.05; an estimation fails if the confidence interval is too wide for a decision. The plan does both without separating them.
issues.what_breaks: The analyst finishes the backtest and says 'in 6 of 10 prior shortage cycles, backlog converted at high rates; in 4 of 10, it did not. That is mixed.' Is that a failed hypothesis test (binary not confirmed) or evidence that you need to estimate the conditional probability and the stock market prices it? The plan does not clarify. The research committee will ask 'is this a buy or a test?' and get a non-answer.
issues.fix: Decide: is this a signal validation (does shortage guidance correlate with forward returns)? Or is this a valuation call (what is the fair price given the backlog/LTA, and is the market lower)? Produce one or the other, not both. For a systematic firm, signal validation is the right frame; for a single-name call it is valuation. This plan is written as if for a fundamental manager but scheduled as if for a quant. Pick one.

issues.summary: The plan describes pitfalls (double-ordering, enforcement renegotiation, reflexivity) but treats them as hygiene—things to watch—rather than as real problems that could flip the conclusion.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The reflexivity point is critical: a shortage guidance announcement *induces* LTA signing because customers fear future allocation. The model counts the LTAs as evidence of durable demand, but they may be an artifact of the shortage itself, not proof that demand persists after the shortage clears. In other words, you might be measuring fear, not fundamentals. The enforcement point is also real: take-or-pay clauses almost never get enforced; customers invoke 'force majeure', negotiate discounts, or settle for a fraction of the damage. Using the stated damages as a haircut is optimistic. These are not pitfalls; they are reasons the model might overestimate durability.
issues.what_breaks: In the validation backtest, you find that backlog converted well during the shortage period and 12 months after, but then reverted as customers who signed 'just in case' cancelled or delayed. Your model called it durable; it was not.
issues.fix: Separate LTAs signed *before* the shortage guidance (which are structural) from those signed *during/after* (which are reactionary). They predict very differently. Test the two separately in the backtest. If reactionary LTAs convert at 30% vs. 70% for pre-shortage ones, say so and adjust your estimate. Do not lump them.

issues.summary: The plan checks a lot of places where it could be wrong mechanically (inventory rising, definition drift, implied bookings negative) but does not check the most basic question: do the companies in the prior shortage episodes that have high haircut-adjusted committed revenue *actually outperform*?
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan builds the measurement framework (tiered haircuts, agreement scoring, RPO reconciliation) and assumes that if the measurement is good, the return will follow. But the return is the question. Before doing any of that work, the backtest should ask: of the 20 semiconductor companies in 2021–22 shortage, did those with the *highest* backlog-to-revenue ratio outperform? Did those with high announced LTA value outperform? Did those with customer prepayments outperform? A simple cross-sectional sort (quintile returns) on raw backlog, LTA count, and cash support, across the prior cycles, should be step one. If that sort shows nothing, haircuts will not create a signal from noise. If it shows something, *then* optimize the measurement.
issues.what_breaks: The analyst spends 6 weeks engineering haircuts and scenario models. Then they backtest and find that raw backlog and LTA count predict 0% return difference across quintiles. The engineered version will not work because the raw signal is not there.
issues.fix: Precede everything with a crude backtest: does backlog-to-revenue ratio quintile (top quintile vs. bottom) predict forward returns in the prior 5 shortage cycles? Does LTA dollar value? Does the presence of customer cash/prepay? Run this in 2–3 days. If quintile spread is >5% annualized, proceed to engineering. If it is <2%, stop.

issues.summary: The reverse DCF and 'EV does not price that' claim compares the stock price to a modeled intrinsic value, but does not account for the risk that the durability model itself is wrong, causing the stock to deserveits current price despite the analyst's view.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan computes: haircut-adjusted committed revenue → model forward cash flows → terminal value → DCF to today → compare to market cap. If the market cap is lower, the stock is cheap. But the comparison assumes: (1) the haircut-adjusted model is right, (2) the terminal margin assumptions are right, (3) the cost of capital is right. If the market has different assumptions on any of these (e.g., a tighter haircut because enforcement is weaker, or a lower terminal margin because scale is harder), then the market price is not wrong—it is different. A DCF that does not enumerate its assumptions and compare to market-embedded ones does not prove mispricing, only that two models diverge.
issues.what_breaks: The analyst builds a DCF valuing the stock at $85, market is at $70, calls it 20% upside. The market, however, is already modeling 50% haircut-adjusted committed revenue (you use 65%), so the market price is consistent with the market's view, not a miss. Your model is not better, just different. If you don't measure the market's implicit model first, you cannot tell these apart.
issues.fix: Reverse-engineer the market price into a model: at the current stock price, what haircut on committed revenue is the market assuming? What terminal margin? What growth rate post-shortage? Then compare your explicit assumptions to the market-implied ones. 'Our model assumes 65% haircut, market implies 45%, so we see 20% upside' is an edge statement. 'Our model is at $85, market is at $70' is not, unless you show the difference is model error, not assumption difference.

issues.summary: The plan does not state how quickly the first usable output could be delivered, or what a minimal version would look like. It is scheduled as a full end-to-end build with all robustness checks.
issues.why_it_applies_here: A systematic firm wants to know: how fast could we trade this signal? If the answer is 'not for three months', the firm may not care—the opportunity will have decayed, the thesis will have been tested by others, or the signal will be too crowded to have capacity. The plan should state: 'minimal version (raw backlog sort across cohort) takes 10 days; if promising, we add LTA scoring (add 15 days); if that works, we add scenario modeling (add 15 days).' This is an adaptive plan. The current plan is a cascade.
issues.what_breaks: Three months from now, the analyst delivers the perfect model. The stock has already rallied 25% on the guidance. The thesis has been crowded by 30 other funds doing the same analysis. Capacity is gone.
issues.fix: Reorder as a series of gates: (1) Crude backlog sort (10 days), (2) LTA value backtest (15 days), (3) cash/prepay impact (10 days), (4) scenario modeling (20 days). Stop after each gate if the result is negative. Commit to delivery of a tradable signal within 30 days of start, even if it is rough.

result.overall: This plan is a sophisticated single-name earnings investigation that would be excellent for a concentrated fundamental manager, but it is misdirected for a systematic trading firm. It reads as confirming a thesis (shortage → durable revenue → upside) rather than discovering one, lacks a pre-committed falsifier and edge statement, gates the output behind six conditions simultaneously (inviting mechanical rejection), requires weeks of bespoke analyst work before testing whether the raw signal even exists, and is too opaque for independent replication. The firm should either: (1) reframe this as a systematic signal (does shortage guidance, measured simply, predict forward returns across a cohort?) and backtest it before optimizing, or (2) acknowledge it as a one-off fundamental call and route it to a concentrated portfolio team. Forcing it through as a quant plan wastes weeks on engineering when the fundamental question—does the market price this already, and does the raw effect exist?—has not been answered yet.

result.plan_implied_asker: A systematic trading firm, days-to-week horizon, signal-centric, cost and crowding conscious, production-ready with replication infrastructure.
result.what_would_falsify: Episodes where contracted price stayed materially above spot for 8+ quarters post-normalization, absent a hard qualification moat. Additionally, pre-registered thresholds for the live HBM case (contract-liability direction, RPO growth, customs tracking, customer obligation-table increases) checkable within 12 months.

issues.summary: Ordinal coding of outcomes (volume and price separation at T+4/8/12) lacks a continuous metric linking observed behavior to the haircut that would actually move the signal.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan outputs 'a probability-weighted haircut, not a verdict,' but the coding scheme (ordinal ranks by feature) cannot produce a continuous estimate of repricing speed or magnitude. Base rates by feature tell you *which* contracts break, but not *how much* of the stated price premium evaporates. For a systematic firm with transaction-cost budgets, the signal is worthless unless it quantifies expected repricing within a horizon, which ordinal bucketing does not deliver.
issues.what_breaks: The validation step will identify which episode features predict durability, but the actual trading signal—how many basis points to fade the multiple for this company given its contract book—remains unspecified. A committee re-running this cannot produce a sizing rule or a capacity allocation.
issues.fix: Convert ordinal outcomes to a continuous measure: either repricing speed (months to revert X% of gap) or price haircut at each quarter, regressed on the contract features and capacity-ledger variables. The result is defensible as a reduced-form estimate, not a true causal effect, which is appropriate for signal work. Alternatively, if the ordinal approach is retained, output a worked example showing how a specific company's contract disclosure maps to a specific haircut assumption, with the reasoning explicit enough a researcher can replicate it on the next case.

issues.summary: The capacity ledger—the 'key predictor'—is introduced but not operationalized: no specification of how to compute the gap, weight contracts by maturity, or flag 'hidden capacity.'
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan correctly identifies that the gap between supply-demand balance and weighted-average LTA maturity drives outcomes, and it is ranked as the top predictor. However, the data sources (SEMI fab database, capex guidance) are industry-standard and often stale or opaque. The method says 'build a capacity ledger' without saying whether this is a quarterly snapshot, a forward-extrapolation using ramp curves, or a survey-based reconstruction. For a systematic firm, this is not a minor methodological choice—it determines whether the signal updates in real time (quarterly capex guidance) or lags (once public fab data is available). The plan must specify the data frequency, the lag structure, and how 'hidden capacity' (pre-announced or unannounced fabs) is detected and treated.
issues.what_breaks: Without an operationalized capacity ledger, the ranking by feature cannot be executed, and the holdout validation cannot be run. The researcher will hit this step with ambiguity about whether to use point-in-time SEMI data, extrapolate from capex, or wait for shipment evidence—each choice will produce different orderings and either forward-bias (using later data at T=0) or temporal misalignment.
issues.fix: Pre-specify the capacity ledger build: (a) data source hierarchy (point-in-time fab database as baseline, capex guidance to extrapolate forward ramps, customs shipment data to detect hidden/early capacity), (b) the weighting scheme for LTA maturity (duration-weighted, or bucketed into near/medium/far terms), (c) the update frequency and look-ahead rules (no capex data or fab counts dated after T=0), (d) a test reconciliation on a historical case (e.g., polysilicon 2007-2012) to show the ledger would have predicted the overhang correctly.

issues.summary: Disclosure asymmetry (signature announced, unwind silent) is listed in pitfalls but not tested as a formal negative control.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan acknowledges that LTA announcements are marketed as bullish (they signal durability) while quiet renegotiations or breaches are not disclosed symmetrically, biasing the episode sample toward apparent durability. This is a real selection effect—a researcher coding outcomes from 10-K disclosures will see the LTA on the books and miss the quiet price repricing unless they cross-check against supplier margins or customer purchase-obligation tables. The plan lists this as a pitfall but does not operationalize a check: for each episode, there should be a step that flags whether unwind was detected silently or not, then tests whether detected-versus-silent episodes have different apparent durability.
issues.what_breaks: The base rates computed in step (4) will be biased toward durability if unwinding was silent in cases coded as durable. This biases the holdout prediction upward. For the HBM case, if a repricing occurs quietly (e.g., via index pass-through or side agreements not in Exhibit 10), the pre-registered checks (contract-liability direction, RPO growth) might miss it, leading to a false forecast of durability.
issues.fix: For each episode, add a detectability flag: whether repricing evidence appears in (a) supplier 10-K margin footnotes, (b) customer purchase-obligation-table dollar reductions, (c) shipment prices (Panjiva), (d) legal filings. Compute base rates separately for high-detectability episodes (where silent unwind is unlikely) versus low-detectability (where margin changes are the only signal). For HBM, pre-register a margin check on Samsung/SK Hynix/Micron quarterly earnings as a supplementary falsifier alongside the contractual checks.

issues.summary: The framework is tested on held-out 2021-2024 auto-semi data, but this is the wrong holdout: the auto-semi cycle was dominated by demand-shock recovery, not supply-normalization from a shortage-born LTA book.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan correctly identifies that 'conflating demand-driven shortage-in-growth with supply-shock-in-flat-demand' is likely the dominant variance driver, then uses 2021-2024 auto semis as validation. This is the worst possible holdout for testing the theory. In 2021-2024, demand recovered sharply (EV ramp, China stimulus through 2021-2022, industrial capex), masking whether LTA repricing occurred or was simply overwhelmed by volume upside. A contract repricing undetected because customers were expanding total purchases is not a confirmation of durability—it is a confound. The framework needs to be validated on an episode where demand was flat or declining *during* the repricing period, making price moves visible.
issues.what_breaks: The holdout validation will show that auto-semi LTAs 'held' through 2024, but this tells the committee nothing about whether they held because customers valued the volume or because demand was expanding faster than supply, masking repricing. When demand normalizes post-2024, the test may fail. This is a validity failure that only surfaces later.
issues.fix: Use polysilicon 2007-2012 as the holdout instead. Demand for polysilicon collapsed in 2008-2009 (solar demand crashed), stayed flat through 2010-2011, and recovered only in 2012-2013. This forces the framework to predict repricing in a flat-to-declining demand environment, where price cuts cannot be hidden by volume growth. Build the framework on 20-25 other episodes (memory, LNG, containers, passives, lithium), then pre-register predictions for polysilicon with dates before checking. Alternatively, identify another historical episode (LNG 2008-2015, uranium 2008-2016) where demand was weak during the repricing window.

issues.summary: The hypothesis distinguishes durability by switching cost and qualification lag, but does not test whether label predicts switching cost, or whether the stated mechanism is the real one.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan correctly ranks outcomes by qualification lag (aerospace/LNG durable, MLCC/containers fragile) and treats the mechanism as switching-cost-driven repricing. However, it does not explicitly test whether qualification lag is proxying for something else—e.g., customer financial health, supplier leverage, or the presence of price-adjustment clauses. Titanium/aero forgings may hold not because requalification is hard, but because aerospace OEMs are solvent with long runways and suppliers have less distress incentive. Containers may break not because requalification is cheap, but because shipping lines are price-takers in commodity markets with no bargaining power. The plan should include a step testing whether the mechanism is indeed switching cost or whether it is merely correlated with it.
issues.what_breaks: The framework will predict that a company with high qualification-lag products will see durable LTAs, but the edge may be spurious if the real driver is credit quality or market structure. When a company with low-credit qualifications in high-switchcost industries faces pressure, the model will miss repricing risk.
issues.fix: For each episode, separately code: switching cost (binary: requalification lag in months), customer credit (rating or default probability), supplier bargaining power (HHI, recent pricing disputes), and market structure (spot-market transparency, number of viable suppliers). Rank outcomes against each predictor independently, not just against the label. Identify cases where switching cost is high but repricing occurs anyway (signals the mechanism is not the dominant one) or where switching cost is low but durability holds (signals robustness or a confound). This is one more data-coding step per episode, not a major addition.

issues.summary: The pre-registration for HBM uses a 12-month window, but HBM shortage normalization may take 18-24 months, pushing the falsifier beyond the decision horizon.
issues.why_it_applies_here: HBM supply was tight in 2023 and was expected to normalize in 2025-2026. The plan pre-registers checks within 12 months (by end of 2024), but by then the shortage may not have fully cleared, so contract repricing will not be visible. A durable-looking contract in 12 months may reprice in months 13-18, after the signal has been acted upon and the check is no longer useful. For a systematic firm with a days-to-weeks horizon, the falsifier must produce a decision-relevant result before the trade ages out.
issues.what_breaks: The HBM check may return inconclusive (RPO still growing, no repricing visible at 12 months), leaving the committee unable to judge success or failure. The framework remains live but untested. Alternatively, if repricing is slow (asymmetric to polysilicon or containers), the 12-month window may not be long enough to falsify the theory, even if it is wrong.
issues.fix: Either (a) extend the pre-registered window to 18 months or set a decision rule for inconclusive cases (e.g., 'if RPO is still growing and repricing is not evident by month 12, we assume durability and proceed; if it drops sharply between 12-18 months, update the model'), or (b) use a proxy that moves faster—e.g., quarterly gross margin by product mix (HBM vs. commodity DRAM), supply-chain pricing indices, or customer earnings-call language shifts to spot-based language. The choice depends on whether HBM repricing is truly slow (suggesting the framework is less applicable) or whether the signal just needs an earlier marker.

issues.summary: Customs/bill-of-lading data (Panjiva, ImportGenius) are proposed as a price signal, but these platforms do not reliably capture unit prices for semiconductors, and coverage is sparse for internal transfers and specialty suppliers.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan uses shipment data as a tiebreaker when supplier, customer, and price-index data disagree ('where they disagree, shipment data wins'). For semiconductors, import data from Panjiva or ImportGenius has two weaknesses: (1) HS codes for semis are broad and do not separate pricing tiers (HBM vs. DRAM, aerospace-qualified vs. commercial), so unit values are noisy; (2) many semiconductor flows are internal transfers (fab-to-assembly, parent-to-subsidiary) or complex supply chains (design-to-fabless-to-foundry-to-customer) that do not always appear in customs filings. For polysilicon or chemicals, this works better; for semis, it is unreliable. The plan overstates the authority of shipment data.
issues.what_breaks: In cases where price indices, supplier 10-Ks, and customs unit values disagree, the tiebreaker (customs) may be noisy, leading to miscoding of whether repricing occurred. This is most likely to matter in cases with opaque supply chains (HBM qualification chains, niche aerospace semis) where customs data is sparse.
issues.fix: Explicitly test the validity of customs-derived unit prices by comparing them to market-price series (TrendForce, Fastmarkets) for a subset of episodes where both are available (e.g., polysilicon, MLCC). Compute the correlation and error magnitude. If customs unit values diverge from spot by >15-20% on average, reduce their weight in the tiebreaker or use them only for directional confirmation, not as the primary signal. For HBM and specialty semis, note that customs data may not be informative and rely instead on supplier margin disclosures and customer obligation tables.

issues.summary: The analysis does not account for index pass-through clauses—a standard provision in LTAs that allows suppliers to pass through commodity-index moves to customers without renegotiating the headline price.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan lists 'index pass-through masking real price cuts' as a pitfall but does not code for it. Many LTAs, especially in chemicals and commodities (polysilicon, lithium offtakes), include cost-based pricing formulas that track spot indices. A supplier can hold the headline price while spot drops and the index component falls, creating the appearance of durability when the effective price (index-adjusted) has repriced. The framework must separate contracts with fixed price from those with index-linked price to avoid miscoding durability.
issues.what_breaks: Episodes with index-linked pricing will be coded as durable based on headline-price stability, when the effective repricing has already occurred. Base rates for 'durable' will be inflated for commodity LTAs. The framework will misidentify which types of contracts truly hold.
issues.fix: When coding contracts (step 2), flag whether pricing is fixed, index-linked (with specific formula), or formula-plus-fixed-spread. When coding outcomes (step 3), for index-linked contracts, compute the realized price including the index adjustment, not the headline contract price. Compute base rates separately for fixed-price and index-linked contracts; they predict different things and should not be pooled.

issues.summary: The framework ranks features without testing interaction effects: high switching cost with weak credit, or high qualification lag in a structurally oversupplied market.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The plan proposes to rank outcomes by feature (qualification lag, sourcing, credit, pricing) separately, not regressed (step 4). This is appropriate for a small sample (20-30 episodes), but it means interactions cannot be detected. A company with high switching cost in a normally-supplied market may reprice faster than one with moderate switching cost in a tight market. The framework will miss these dependencies, producing inflated uncertainty ranges.
issues.what_breaks: The probability-weighted haircut output will have wider error bars than necessary, reducing signal precision. In borderline cases (medium switching cost, medium supply slack), the framework will be less confident than the data supports.
issues.fix: Test a few key interactions explicitly: (a) switching cost × excess capacity (does high switching cost fail to hold when the supplier is desperately oversupplied?), (b) credit quality × switching cost (do weak customers break even high-switchcost contracts?). Document which interactions were tested and how they change the predicted outcome for the live case. This is a few additional comparisons, not a regression, and defensible at a research committee.

issues.summary: The definition of 'durability' is ordinal (held volume/price at T+4/8/12) rather than a continuous measure of repricing speed, making it impossible to compute a signal that distinguishes between 'mostly durable' and 'quickly repriced.'
issues.why_it_applies_here: The outcome coding uses an ordinal scale, which tells you whether repricing happened, but not *how fast*. For a systematic firm pricing a stock, knowing that 70% of high-switchcost contracts reprice within 6 months is more actionable than knowing they eventually do. The plan outputs a 'probability-weighted haircut,' but without a continuous repricing-speed distribution, the haircut is a binary guess, not a ranged estimate. A quant researcher would need repricing-speed quantiles (20th, 50th, 80th percentile months-to-reprice) to size a position and set a holding horizon.
issues.what_breaks: The signal output will be a point estimate of haircut, with wide confidence bands due to small sample size. The committee cannot assess whether to apply a 50bps or 150bps haircut, or whether to fade a stock for 3 months or 12 months.
issues.fix: Retain the ordinal coding but additionally compute, for each outcome, the number of quarters (or months, if data permits) until the first detectable repricing event (margin drop, price index reversal, customer obligation-table reduction). This gives a continuous measure of 'time to first repricing,' which can be aggregated by feature and used to produce a ranged output: 'high-switchcost contracts with 80%+ confidence reprice by quarter Q+X, 50% by Q+Y.' This is not a prediction of exactly when, but a cumulative-probability distribution that a PM can use to size horizon.

issues.summary: The sample is curated to episodes where large LTAs were announced; survivorship bias is listed as a pitfall but no correction is proposed.
issues.why_it_applies_here: The episode list (polysilicon, auto semis, memory, MLCC, ABF, uranium, LNG, containers, lithium, titanium) is drawn from suppliers with notable LTA announcements or litigation. This biases toward large, transparent suppliers and famous shortages. Smaller suppliers who signed LTAs and repriced silently, or who failed entirely (exiting the market), do not appear in the sample. For a systematic signal, this creates a survivorship bias: the framework will overstate the durability of LTAs because it is more likely to observe and remember the ones that held than the ones that triggered supplier distress or exit.
issues.what_breaks: Base rates will be inflated for 'durable' outcomes. The framework will produce a higher haircut than is justified if applied to smaller, less-capitalized suppliers or to future shortages where supplier exits are a real path.
issues.fix: For each episode, explicitly document whether surviving suppliers had large, disclosed LTA books (sampled here), or whether there were smaller suppliers with LTA books that repriced or exited. Adjust the base rates for survivorship by comparing the fraction of suppliers in the episode that are in the sample to the fraction of total supply they represented. Alternatively, note the survivorship assumption and test its effect: compute base rates for high-survivorship episodes (large suppliers, well-documented) separately from low-survivorship ones. For the live case (HBM), explicitly monitor for supplier exits or margin compression as a secondary falsifier alongside the pre-registered checks.

issues.summary: The framework does not distinguish between repricing via contract amendment (explicit) and repricing via non-enforcement (implicit), which have different mechanisms and predictability.
issues.why_it_applies_here: When LTAs reprice, they can do so via: (1) formal renegotiation and contract amendment (explicit, visible in filings if disclosed), (2) supplier threatening litigation and customer settling at a new price (semi-explicit, visible in litigation filings), (3) supplier simply not enforcing take-or-pay and customers quietly reducing volumes (implicit, visible only in margin/obligation tables). The framework codes outcomes as binary (price held or repriced) but does not distinguish mechanism. Implicit repricing via non-enforcement is invisible to market prices and may be the most common path. The framework will miss it unless explicitly looking for margin deterioration or obligation-table compression.
issues.what_breaks: Episodes where repricing occurred implicitly (supplier gave in, quietly, without renegotiation) will be miscoded as 'durable' if the headline contract language did not change. Base rates will overstate durability. For the HBM case, if repricing occurs via Samsung or TSMC simply reducing high-priced orders (without amending the contract), the pre-registered checks (contract-liability direction, RPO) might miss it if RPO stays on the books but customers simply don't draw it.
issues.fix: For each episode, flag the repricing mechanism: formal amendment, litigation settlement, implicit non-enforcement (inferred from margin drops or obligation-table changes). Compute base rates separately for each mechanism type. Add a secondary outcome measure: customer purchase-obligation-table absolute change (not percentage), which captures quiet demand destruction. For HBM, monitor for a divergence between RPO growth and actual shipment volumes (from customs/Panjiva): if RPO grows but shipments flatten, non-enforcement is likely.

result.overall: This is a well-conceived research plan for a systematic firm, with a clear mechanism (switching-cost-driven repricing), appropriate sample selection (20-30 historical episodes spanning industries), and a falsifiable hypothesis (repriced episodes should cluster by qualification lag, not label). The design appropriately front-loads the capacity ledger as the key predictor, uses pre-registration for the live HBM case, and tests negative controls (aerospace and containers as ordinal bounds). The firm fit is excellent: the plan respects the horizon (days-to-weeks signal), assumes production infrastructure (customs data, legal filings, ML-based contract coding), and outputs something a committee can re-run (ordinal codes, episode tables, base rates). Error asymmetry is correct for a Type II setting (breadth, signal-focused): a missed real repricing effect is the expensive mistake, and the burden of proof is appropriately modest. The plan would deliver a probability-weighted haircut, not a true causal effect, which is the right output for a signal. However, the plan has two blocking issues and several secondary ones. The capacity ledger—called the key predictor—is never operationalized; the plan must specify data sources, update frequency, and how to weight LTA maturities before validation can run. The auto-semi holdout is wrong: demand was booming during the repricing window, confounding durability with volume growth. Use polysilicon (weak demand 2008-2011) or another flat-demand episode instead. Secondary issues are fixable: the ordinal outcome coding needs a continuous repricing-speed measure to produce a usable signal; disclosure asymmetry needs a detectability flag; the customs-data tiebreaker is overstated and should be validated first; index pass-through should be coded separately; and the framework should test whether switching cost is the real mechanism or a correlate. The plan is ambitious and sound in structure, but cannot be executed until the capacity ledger is specified and the holdout sample is corrected.
